fields.title: The Key Teachings of Watchman Nee
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Watchman Nee's ministry — the normal Christian life as Christ living in the believer, the finished work of the cross, and the way of the overcomers. Eighteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion to Nee's ministry, naming his books for the reader's own further study.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to Watchman Nee, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in eighteen short chapters the teaching for which Nee is chiefly remembered — the normal Christian life as Christ living in the believer, the finished work of the cross, the release of the spirit through the breaking of the outer man, and the way of the overcomers.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation. It is not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any organisation that holds rights in the writings of Watchman Nee. All descriptions of his teaching are the present author's own summaries; his books and spoken ministry are named only for the reader's further study, and readers are warmly encouraged to obtain those works from their rightful publishers. Nothing of Nee's own text is reproduced here — only Scripture, quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and Ochorus's account of what he taught.

Nee taught, more insistently than almost anyone, that no servant of God is to be looked at. The right response to his ministry is not admiration but obedience — not to him, but to the Lord he spent his life trying to describe.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. JOHN 12:24

There is a kind of Christian teaching that adds information to the mind. There is another kind that quietly dismantles a man. The ministry of Watchman Nee belongs to the second kind, and that is why, more than fifty years after he died in a labour camp in Anhwei province, his words are still read in languages he never spoke, in countries he never visited, by believers who were not born when he was buried. He was not a systematic theologian, and he would have been uneasy at being called one. He wrote no volume of dogmatics, founded no seminary, and left behind no confession of faith bearing his name. What he left behind was something both smaller and larger: a body of spoken ministry, taken down by listeners and afterwards gathered into books, which pressed a single question upon the conscience of the believer. The question was not What ought I to do for God? It was What has God already done, and am I willing to stand upon it? That question runs like a seam of ore through everything he taught. It is there in The Normal Christian Life, where he laboured to show that Romans chapters six to eight are not a counsel of effort but a declaration of accomplished fact. It is there in Sit, Walk, Stand, where the Christian’s whole conduct and warfare are made to rest upon a prior resting. It is there in The Release of the Spirit, where the great hindrance to fruitfulness is located not in the believer’s weakness but in his unbroken strength. And it is there, most painfully, in the last twenty years of his life, when the man who had taught the church about the cross was himself required to bear one.

This book is an attempt to set out, in eighteen short chapters, the teaching for which Watchman Nee is chiefly remembered. It is written for the ordinary believer — the pastor with more congregations than books, the student who has heard the name and wants to know what the fuss is about, the professional who is respected at church and quietly defeated at home, the believer who has been trying for years to live the Christian life and has begun to suspect he is going about it the wrong way entirely. A word about how to use it. Each chapter is deliberately short, and each one ends in the same two places: a set of application points, and a prayer. This is not decoration. Nee held, with some force, that spiritual truth which is merely understood has not yet been received at all. He was fond of pointing out that revelation in Scripture is almost always followed immediately by demand. The Lord shows a man something, and then requires something of him. A chapter of this book that is read and admired but not obeyed has, by its own argument, failed. Read one chapter a day, or one a week. Stop at the application points. Pray the prayer, or better, pray your own. A word also about the limits of this book. It is a summary, and every summary is a kind of flattening. Nee’s actual ministry is richer, stranger and more uneven than any digest of it can be, and there is no substitute for going to the works themselves. Throughout these pages his own books and spoken addresses are named, so that the reader may follow any thread back to its source. A short guide to those works is provided at the end.

One more thing must be said at the outset, and it is better said plainly. This is not a book of hero-worship. Watchman Nee was a man, and the record of his life contains matters that are painful, contested and, in some particulars, probably unknowable this side of eternity. There were seasons of controversy among his own co-workers. There was a period of some six years in which he withdrew from the Lord’s Table. When the state finally tried him in 1956, the charges laid against him included moral and financial ones; his defenders have always insisted these were manufactured by a hostile government determined to destroy his credibility, while some careful historians have concluded that not all of them were. The trial was conducted under a regime that had every interest in his ruin, which makes the evidence extremely difficult to weigh at this distance. The reader may be tempted to ask why a book of this kind would raise such a matter at all. The answer is that Nee himself would have insisted upon it. No teaching was more central to him than that the flesh — including the religious flesh, including the gifted and useful and admired flesh — is utterly untrustworthy and must go to the cross. A book that presented him as a spotless saint would be contradicting the very doctrine it was written to commend. So the counsel of this book is the counsel of Scripture: Prove all things; hold fast that which is good (1 Thessalonians 5:21). Weigh every chapter against the Word of God. Where Nee is faithful to Scripture — and on the great themes of the cross, of union with Christ, of consecration and brokenness and the Body, he is very faithful indeed — receive it gladly and act upon it. Where he presses beyond what is written, and there are places where he does, mark it, set it aside, and lose nothing.

Truth is not damaged by being carried in an earthen vessel. That, after all, is the only kind of vessel God has ever used.

One final observation, which may explain why this particular ministry has travelled as far as it has. Watchman Nee wrote in Chinese, for Chinese believers, in a country sliding into war. He never intended a worldwide readership and would very likely have been embarrassed by one. Yet his books have crossed nearly every border that exists, and are read today in languages he never heard spoken, by Christians whose circumstances have nothing in common with his own. The reason is not literary. It is that he dealt almost exclusively with what does not vary. Cultures differ enormously in what they prize, permit and punish; the human heart is depressingly uniform. Self-reliance, the instinct to earn, the reluctance to be broken, the preference for governing oneself — these require no translation. A believer in a wealthy suburb and a believer in a village without electricity are further apart in circumstance than almost any two people in history, and they are wrestling with precisely the same man in the mirror. So this book assumes no particular setting. Wherever it is read, and into whatever language it is carried, the questions it raises will already be waiting. There is also this. Nee did not teach the deeper life from a position of comfort. He taught it to workers who would shortly be scattered, and he sealed it by returning to Shanghai in 1949 when he could have stayed away, and by refusing, through twenty years of imprisonment, to purchase his freedom by denying his Lord. A man may teach the cross with his mouth. Nee was required to teach it with his life. That is why we still listen.

fields.title: A Life Poured Out
fields.body_html:
I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith. 2 TIMOTHY 4:7

The child who was asked for. He was born on the fourth of November, 1903, in the coastal city of Swatow, in southern China, and given the name Ni Shu-tsu. His father, Ni Weng-hsiu, was an officer in the Imperial Customs Service; his grandfather, Ni Yu-cheng, had been among the earliest Chinese to be ordained as a Protestant preacher in Fukien province. The family was Christian, respectable and Methodist, and the boy was baptised as an infant by a Methodist bishop. His mother, Lin Ho-ping — Peace Lin — had borne two daughters and desperately wanted a son. In the manner of Hannah at Shiloh she vowed that if God gave her a boy she would give him back. God gave her a boy. It would be nearly eighteen years before either of them understood what the vow had cost. The child was brilliant. He read early, argued well, and swept the prizes at the mission school in Foochow where the family had returned to live. He was also, by his own later account, a thoroughly worldly young man — clever, ambitious, contemptuous of the religion of his parents, and privately determined to make a name in the world. Christianity he regarded as a sentimental encumbrance suited to women and the elderly.

April 1920. In the spring of 1920 a Chinese evangelist named Dora Yu came to Foochow to preach. Dora Yu had trained in medicine and abandoned it for the gospel; she was a Methodist, a woman of prayer, and she preached with a directness that cut. Peace Lin went to the meetings. What happened to her there was so thorough that she came home and did something no Chinese mother of that generation would ordinarily do: she apologised to her son for a wrong she had done him. It undid him. He went to hear the preacher for himself. On the evening of the twenty-ninth of April, 1920, alone in his room, seventeen years old, he surrendered to Jesus Christ. The change was immediate and total. He began at once to witness — to classmates, to teachers, to anyone within reach — and he drew up a list of some seventy friends whom he undertook to pray for, in some seasons every hour of the day. Before long he changed his name. Ni Shu-tsu became Ni To-sheng: the sound of the watchman’s rattle, the night-watch clapper struck in the darkness to rouse a sleeping town. In English he would be known for the rest of his life as Watchman Nee.

The teacher he needed. He went first to Shanghai to train under Dora Yu and was sent home again, having proved an undisciplined student. It was Dora Yu who then pointed him toward the woman who would shape him more than any other. Margaret E. Barber was an Englishwoman in her fifties who had come out with the Church Missionary Society, returned to England under a cloud of accusation she refused to defend herself against, and come back to China as an independent missionary answerable to no board and supported by no salary. She lived simply at White Teeth Rock, near Pagoda Anchorage on the Min River, and she took the brilliant young convert in hand. She was severe with him. She let him wait; she rebuked him; she declined to flatter a gift that everyone else was already praising. He would say afterwards that she taught him the cross by administering it. She also opened her bookshelves. Through Margaret Barber, Nee met the writers who would furnish his theology for life: the Brethren expositors — Darby, Mackintosh, Robert Govett, G. H. Pember, D. M. Panton; the Keswick and deeper-life authors — Andrew Murray, Jessie Penn-Lewis, Evan Roberts, F. B. Meyer; and the older mystics, above all Madame Guyon, whose little treatise on prayer he would translate into Chinese. In 1921 he was baptised by immersion, having concluded that his infant baptism was no baptism at all. Margaret Barber died in 1930 and left him her few possessions.

Ministry, illness, and the little flock. From 1922 he and a handful of friends began breaking bread together in Foochow, outside the denominational structures, as simply the church in that place. Others joined. The movement that grew from those meetings would be known to outsiders as the Little Flock, and to its own members as the Christian Assembly, or more plainly the church in whatever city it happened to be. By the time of his arrest thirty years later there were some four hundred such assemblies across China, and others in Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand. He began publishing almost at once. His periodicals — The Present Testimony and The Christian — carried his exposition to readers far beyond the reach of his voice. Then his health broke. From the middle of the 1920s he was gravely ill with tuberculosis, for long stretches unable to walk across a room, repeatedly given up by his doctors. It was in this condition, expecting to die, that he wrote his first major work. The Spiritual Man, three volumes on the threefold constitution of man, was published in 1928. He later said the labour of it had cost him more than it was worth, and cautioned readers against making a system out of what he had written — but the book established him. In 1927 the work moved to Shanghai, which became its centre.

Abroad. He travelled to the West twice. In 1933 he visited England and met the Exclusive Brethren, whose literature had formed him and whose exclusivism afterwards led them to break with him. He also spent time at Honor Oak in south London with T. Austin-Sparks, who became a friend. The second visit, in 1938 and 1939, was the more consequential. Speaking in England, Denmark and elsewhere in Europe on the eve of the war, he gave the series of addresses on Romans that were afterwards gathered, edited and published as The Normal Christian Life. It remains, by a wide margin, the book by which the English-speaking world knows him. In 1934 he had married Charity Chang, whom he had known since childhood; the marriage drew criticism from some quarters and cost him friendships.

The wilderness years. In 1942 the work suffered a rupture. Nee had become involved in a pharmaceutical business, the China Biological and Chemical Laboratories, founded with his brother, intending its profits to support the workers. The elders of the Shanghai assembly judged this unbecoming in a servant of God and asked him to cease ministering. He submitted. For roughly six years he did not break bread with the church he had raised up, and did not preach. Those years are variously interpreted. His defenders describe a humble submission to misguided brethren. Others, including some who knew him, believed his own conscience was involved. He himself said little. In 1948 he was restored to fellowship, and there followed the most remarkable period of his teaching ministry: the trainings for workers held on Kuling Mountain, near Foochow, in 1948 and 1949. Out of those sessions came Spiritual Authority, The Character of God’s Workman, and much else. He also called the believers to hand over — to place their homes, properties and livelihoods at the disposal of the Lord and the church. Many did.

The last chapter. The Communists took the mainland in 1949. Nee was in Hong Kong early in that year, safe, with every opportunity to remain. In February he decided to go back to Shanghai. He understood what he was choosing. For a time the churches continued; the Shanghai assembly still gathered thousands. Then the Three-Self Patriotic Movement was organised, and the pressure to submit the churches to state control became irresistible. Nee would not. He was arrested on the tenth of April, 1952. For four years the believers did not know where he was. In January 1956 he was denounced at a mass accusation meeting in Shanghai, before a crowd that included his own former co-workers, and an indictment of some two thousand pages was published against him. Later that year he was sentenced to fifteen years’ imprisonment. He was never released. When the fifteen years expired in 1967 he was simply kept. It is said that freedom was offered him more than once if he would lead a state-approved church, and that he refused every time. Only his wife was permitted to visit. Charity died on the seventh of November, 1971; he was not allowed to attend her funeral. Watchman Nee died on the thirtieth of May, 1972, at a labour farm in Guangde, in Anhwei province, sixty-eight years old, having spent twenty years in confinement. A grand-niece who came to collect his effects was given a scrap of paper found beneath his pillow, written in his own hand. Its substance was that Christ is the Son of God who died for the redemption of sinners and rose on the third day — and that he, Watchman Nee, died believing it. The watchman had kept his post until the morning.

fields.title: The Normal Christian Life
fields.body_html:
I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. GALATIANS 2:20

Watchman Nee opened his most famous book with a question that sounds almost impertinent. What, he asked, is the normal Christian life? The word matters. He did not ask what the ideal Christian life is, or the advanced Christian life, or the life of those unusual saints whose biographies we read with admiration and no expectation of imitation. He asked what is normal. And he answered that the normal Christian life is the life described in Galatians 2:20 — a life no longer lived by the believer at all, but by Christ in him. Set that beside the experience of most of us and the gap is immediately painful. What we call normal is something else: a cycle of resolve and failure, of conferences that lift us and Mondays that flatten us, of sins confessed on Sunday and committed again by Wednesday. We have quietly redefined normal downward until it means defeated, and then we have comforted ourselves that everyone else is defeated too. Nee’s whole ministry was a protest against this redefinition. The New Testament standard, he insisted in The Normal Christian Life, is not an unreachable summit for the few. It is the ordinary birthright of every child of God. And the reason we do not enjoy it is not that we have not tried hard enough. It is that we have been trying at all.

The two halves of the problem

He built his case on Romans, and he made much of the way that letter is constructed. Romans divides at the end of chapter five. The first section, chapters one to five verse eleven, deals with one problem. The second section, chapter five verse twelve through chapter eight, deals with another. Nee summarised the Christian’s response to the finished work of Christ in a sequence of four words drawn straight from Romans 6, and the order is everything. Know — verse six. Reckon — verse eleven. It is the occupation of a position we already hold.

There is one further thing to say, and Nee said it constantly. This life is not self-improvement. It is substitution. The end of the process is not a better version of you. It is Christ living where you used to live. Not I, but Christ.

The objection arises immediately, and Nee met it directly. If the normal Christian life is Christ living in me, does that mean the believer no longer sins? He also insisted — and this is the safeguard against every form of perfectionism — that the deliverance is never a possession we hold independently of Christ. It is not a state achieved and then owned. It is a moment-by-moment dependence. The branch does not store up sap for later; it draws continuously, and the moment it stops drawing it withers, however green it looked yesterday.

fields.title: The Blood and the Cross
fields.body_html:
The blood of Jesus Christ his Son cleanseth us from all sin. 1 JOHN 1:7

If a man is to understand anything of Watchman Nee’s teaching, he must first grasp a distinction that Nee drew more sharply than almost any teacher before him: the difference between the blood of Christ and the cross of Christ. They are not two events. Calvary is one event. But it accomplishes two different things, addressed to two different problems, and applied in two different ways — and to confuse them is to remain permanently stuck.

The blood deals with what I have done

The blood, Nee taught, is Godward before it is manward. It is not primarily about how I feel; it is about how God is satisfied. Its first witness is not the sinner’s peace but the righteousness of God.

And when I see the blood, I will pass over you. EXODUS 12:13

Observe carefully what the Lord did not say to Israel in Egypt. He did not say, when you see the blood. He did not say, when you feel confident about the blood. He said, when I see the blood. The Israelite inside the house might be trembling; he might be doubting; he might have spent the night in an agony of uncertainty as to whether he had applied it properly. It made no difference whatever to his safety. The blood was on the door, and God was outside looking at it. This is the ground of the believer’s assurance, and Nee returned to it again and again in his gospel ministry and in The Normal Christian Life. Our forgiveness does not rest upon the quality of our repentance, the depth of our sorrow, or the steadiness of our faith. It rests upon a finished transaction which God has accepted. Three things, he said, the blood accomplishes. It satisfies God — it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul (Leviticus 17:11). It cleanses the conscience — how much more shall the blood of Christ …purge your conscience from dead works (Hebrews 9:14). And it silences the accuser — they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb (Revelation 12:11).

That last point deserves attention. Satan is called the accuser of our brethren (Revelation 12:10), and his accusations are frequently true. That is what makes them effective. Nee’s counsel was not to argue with the accuser about the facts, nor to plead one’s improvement, nor to promise to do better. It was to answer every accusation with the blood — to agree that the charge is true and to point to the payment. A debt truly incurred and truly settled is no longer a debt.

The cross deals with what I am

But now suppose a man has received full forgiveness for every sin he has ever committed, and his conscience is entirely at peace. He still has a problem. He will sin again tomorrow. Something in him wants to. Blood cannot touch this. You cannot wash away a nature. The blood addresses the record; the cross addresses the man.

For he that is dead is freed from sin. ROMANS 6:7

God’s answer to what we are is not improvement, reformation or suppression. It is execution. Our old man is crucified with him. God did not send His Son to patch the old creation; He ended it, and began a new one. Nee illustrated the difference with characteristic bluntness. If a man’s clothes are dirty you wash them. If the man himself is incurably diseased, washing his clothes will not help; something must be done with the man. The blood washes; the cross crucifies. To ask the blood to do the cross’s work is like asking soap to cure cancer.

Why the order cannot be reversed

There is a pastoral reason why Nee insisted on keeping these in sequence. Believers who reach for identification with Christ’s death before they are settled in forgiveness will make the cross into a new form of works. They will try to crucify themselves in order to obtain acceptance — which is precisely the treadmill the gospel came to end. First be sure of the blood. Rest wholly there. Let the conscience be purged and the accuser silenced. Then, standing on unshakeable ground, go on to discover what the cross has done with the old man.

Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ …knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him. ROMANS 5:1; 6:6

Peace first. Then deliverance. That is Paul’s order, and Nee would not let his hearers reverse it.

One more observation, because it is easy to miss. Both the blood and the cross are things done to us and for us, not by us. The believer contributes nothing to either but faith. There is no such thing, in Nee’s teaching, as crucifying yourself. Men who attempt it are always found nailing one hand and leaving the other free.

A conscience that will not settle

There is a difficulty that arises for many earnest believers, and Nee dealt with it often, because it troubles the sincere far more than the careless. A man confesses a sin. He knows the promise; he can quote it. And yet the accusation continues. Weeks later the memory surfaces and the old weight descends again, and he confesses once more, and once more, and the matter is never closed. Nee’s diagnosis was blunt: a conscience that keeps condemning what God has cleansed is not being humble. It is being unbelieving.

How much more shall the blood of Christ, who through the eternal Spirit offered himself without spot to God, purge your conscience from dead works to serve the living God? HEBREWS 9:14

The argument of Hebrews turns on this very point. The old sacrifices were repeated endlessly precisely because they could not settle the conscience — for then would they not have ceased to be offered? because that the worshippers once purged should have had no more conscience of sins (Hebrews 10:2). A finished work produces a settled conscience. If our consciences are never settled, it is because we are treating the work as unfinished. He pointed also to Peter on the housetop, told three times to eat what he regarded as unclean, and given a rebuke that applies well beyond its original subject: What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common (Acts 10:15). To keep calling unclean what God has declared clean is not modesty. It is contradiction. The practical counsel that followed was firm. Confess the sin once, thoroughly, naming it. Receive the cleansing. Make restitution where restitution is owed. And then refuse to reopen the file. When the memory returns, do not confess again; instead thank God that it has been dealt with, and turn your attention elsewhere.

Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience. HEBREWS 10:22

Full assurance is not presumption. It is the intended result of the blood.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. When accusation comes this week — and it will — practise answering it in one sentence: That is true, and the blood of Jesus Christ has already paid for it. Do not add promises of improvement. 2. Examine whether your assurance rests on the blood or on your own feelings. Note which one changed most recently. 3. Name one habit or attitude that no amount of forgiveness has ever cured. That is a matter for the cross, not the blood. Bring it to God as such. 4. Read Exodus 12 and Hebrews 9 together this week. Ask what God sees, not what you see. 5. If you have been trying to crucify yourself, stop. Confess it as unbelief, and rest in what was accomplished without you.

A PRAYER
Lord God, I thank You for the blood of Your Son. Not for my sorrow over sin, not for my resolutions, not for my religious performance — for the blood, and the blood alone.
When the accuser comes, teach me to plead nothing else. When my conscience condemns me, remind me that You are greater than my heart and that You have already been satisfied.
And Father, for the sin that lives in me still, show me the cross. I do not ask to be improved. I ask to be brought to an end, that Christ might live where I once did. Amen.

fields.title: In Adam, in Christ
fields.body_html:
For as in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:22

Behind everything Nee taught about deliverance lies a single structural idea, and unless it is grasped the rest will not hold together. It is the idea of the two representative men.

How we got in

Ask a plain question: how did you become a sinner? Most believers, if pressed, will answer that they became sinners by sinning. They committed acts of sin, and those acts made them sinners. Nee argued that this is exactly backwards, and that Romans 5 says so.

Wherefore, as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned …For as by one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one shall many be made righteous. ROMANS 5:12, 19

By one man’s disobedience many were made sinners. Not by their own disobedience — by his. We did not become sinners by sinning; we sin because we were born sinners, and we were born sinners because we were in Adam when he fell. Nee pressed the point with an image from Hebrews. The writer argues that Levi paid tithes to Melchizedek, though Levi was not born for generations, because he was yet in the loins of his father, when Melchisedec met him (Hebrews 7:10). Levi was there, in Abraham, and what Abraham did, Levi did. So with the whole race. We were in Adam. His act was our act. His fall was our fall. This is not a legal fiction that God imposes on us from outside; it is a statement about where we actually were.

How we got out

Now the logic runs the other way, and this is the glory of it. If our ruin came by being in a man, our salvation comes the same way — by being in another Man.

But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:30

Of him are ye in Christ Jesus. It is God’s doing. Nee loved to point out that no one has ever been able to explain how he got into Adam — and no one needs to explain how he got into Christ either. Here Nee drove home the consequence that so many miss. God’s method is not repair. It is replacement.

The old creation in Adam is not being renovated. It has been judged, condemned and terminated at the cross, and a new creation has begun in the risen Christ. Immediately before the great statement of Romans 6:6, Paul appeals to something his readers had all experienced.

fields.title: Know
fields.body_html:
Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with him. ROMANS 6:6

The first of the four words is know, and Nee would not allow anyone to move past it in a hurry. Everything that follows in Romans 6 depends upon it, and nothing that follows can be produced without it. But we must be careful about what kind of knowing is meant, because there are two kinds, and only one of them saves anybody from anything.

Mental grasp and divine revelation

A man may know the doctrine of co-crucifixion perfectly well. He may be able to draw a diagram of it, distinguish it from other views of sanctification, expound the tense of the verb in verse six, and preach a serviceable sermon on it. And he may go home and lose his temper with his wife within the hour. Nee spoke about this constantly, and it forms the substance of his little book Spiritual Knowledge and much of Aids to Revelation. There is knowledge that comes by study, and there is knowledge that comes by revelation, and they are not different amounts of the same thing. They are different in kind.

Blessed art thou, Simon Barjona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 16:17

Peter had said the right words. Others had said them too, or nearly. What the Lord commended was not the accuracy of the sentence but its source. It had not come up from below; it had come down from above. This is why Nee taught believers to pray over their reading — not merely to pray before reading, as a pious formality, but to make the reading itself a matter of asking. The Bible is not a quarry from which the diligent extract truth by labour. It is a place where God speaks to those who wait.

Open thou mine eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of thy law. PSALM 119:18

Why we cannot manufacture it

It follows that revelation cannot be worked up, and Nee was severe about attempts to counterfeit it. You cannot achieve sight by straining.

A blind man who squeezes his eyelids shut and concentrates furiously does not thereby see. He must have light given to him. What then can a believer do? Nee’s answer was: he can ask, and he can be honest, and he can wait. He can ask, because the Lord commands it — ask, and it shall be given you (Matthew 7:7). He can be honest, because revelation is almost always withheld from a man who is unwilling to obey what he already sees. And he can wait, because God’s timing is not ours, and the discovery that comes after long waiting is the one that lasts. He was fond of noting that the great turning points in the lives of believers are rarely the result of a decision to understand. They come suddenly, often during something quite ordinary, and afterwards the person cannot say why he never saw it before, because now he cannot imagine how anyone could miss it. That is the signature of revelation. It does not feel like an achievement. It feels like the removal of something that was in the way.

What we are to know

And what are we to see? Precisely this: that we were included in the death of Jesus Christ. Not that we ought to die. Not that we may die if we are sufficiently consecrated. That we died — finished, accomplished, done.

For ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God. COLOSSIANS 3:3

Nee illustrated it with the difference between a fact and a feeling. Suppose a man is told that a distant relative has died and left him an inheritance. He feels nothing at all; he never knew the relative. But the money is his, whether he feels rich or not. His feelings have no bearing on the estate. What he needs is not emotion but information — and then he must act on it. So with our death in Christ. We do not feel dead. We feel painfully, obviously alive to sin. But the question God puts to us is not how do you feel? It is do you know?

There is a warning to add. Because Nee spoke so much of revelation, some who came after him made a mystique of it, waiting passively for experiences and neglecting the plain labour of reading, memorising and studying the Word. That was never his intention, and his own practice contradicts it. He was a disciplined and omnivorous reader who worked through the Scriptures relentlessly and read widely besides. Revelation does not replace study. It illuminates it. God generally turns on the light in rooms where somebody has been working.

Secondhand light

There is a particular hazard for anyone who reads widely or sits under good teaching, and Nee named it plainly. It is possible to live on other people’s revelation. A believer hears a message that clearly came out of someone’s real dealings with God. He is moved by it. He adopts the language, repeats the illustrations, and begins to teach it himself — having never once seen the thing for himself. What he passes on is a photograph of a meal. It is accurate. It will not nourish anybody. Nee found the principle in the wilderness. The manna had to be gathered every morning by each household, and what was hoarded from the previous day did not keep.

Notwithstanding they hearkened not unto Moses; but some of them left of it until the morning, and it bred worms, and stank. EXODUS 16:20

Yesterday’s supply is not today’s. And another man’s supply is not mine. This accounts, he suggested, for a good deal of preaching that is orthodox, well-arranged, and entirely without weight. The hearers can tell. There is a difference, immediately perceptible and impossible to counterfeit, between a man describing a country he has visited and a man reciting a guidebook. The remedy is not to stop reading. Nee read constantly and urged others to. The remedy is to refuse to pass on as your own what God has not shown you, and to take what you have read back to God until He either confirms it to you or does not. He suggested a discipline that is worth adopting. When a truth strikes you in someone else’s book or sermon, do not immediately use it. Hold it. Bring it to God and ask Him to make it yours, and wait — for days or months if necessary. The truth that has passed through your own experience will come out of you with an authority that borrowed material never has.

That which we have seen and heard declare we unto you. 1 JOHN 1:3

Seen, and heard, and then declared. That is the apostolic order, and there is no shortcut through it.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Before your next Bible reading, ask God plainly for light rather than information. Note the difference in how you read.

2. Identify one truth you can explain but have never experienced. Bring that specific gap before God and ask Him to close it. 3. Check whether disobedience is blocking sight. Is there something you already know to be right and have not done? Do it first. 4. Set aside a longer period — an hour, an afternoon — with Romans 6 and nothing else. No commentary. Ask, and wait. 5. Record the date when God shows you something. Nee’s generation kept such records; the memory of a real dealing with God is a strengthening thing in later drought.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have gathered much information about You, and I am not sure how much of it I have seen. I can explain doctrines that have never changed me. Have mercy on me.
You revealed Yourself to a fisherman who had no learning at all. Flesh and blood did not teach him. Father, teach me in the same way. Open my eyes.
I will not pretend to see what I do not see. But I will wait before You until You show me, and I will obey what You have already shown. Amen.

fields.title: Reckon
fields.body_html:
Likewise reckon ye also yourselves to be dead indeed unto sin, but alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord. ROMANS 6:11

The second word is reckon, and Nee spent a great deal of effort rescuing it from misuse, because it is one of the most misunderstood terms in the New Testament.

Reckoning is not pretending

To reckon, in the ordinary English of the Authorised Version, is to count, to calculate, to enter into the accounts. It is a bookkeeper’s word. It means treating something as true because it is true. What it does not mean is imagining. Nee warned repeatedly against the sort of teaching that tells a believer to repeat I am dead, I am dead until he feels dead, as though repetition could create a fact. That, he said plainly, is not faith; it is self-hypnotism, and it collapses at the first serious temptation. The difference is the ground you are standing on. A man who reckons is standing on something God has said. A man who is pretending is standing on his own determination to believe. When the storm comes, the first man is still standing and the second is not.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

This is why know must come before reckon. You cannot reckon on what you have not seen. Attempting it produces strain, and strain is the surest sign that something has gone wrong. Nee’s rule of thumb was simple: if reckoning has become hard work, go back. You are trying to believe something you have not yet been shown.

Two accounts to keep

Notice that the verse has two halves, and Nee insisted on both. Dead indeed unto sin — that is the negative side. But alive unto God through Jesus Christ our Lord — that is the positive. Christians who attend only to the first become preoccupied with death, introspective and gloomy, forever taking their own spiritual temperature. That is not the apostle’s balance. The purpose of the death is the life. We are not called to be corpses; we are called to be alive to God with an aliveness we did not previously possess.

Nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. GALATIANS 2:20

How reckoning works in a real temptation

Nee was practical about this, and it is worth setting out concretely, because here is where the doctrine either works or does not. Temptation comes. The old response is to fight — to summon willpower, grit the teeth, resolve. And the more we fight in that way, the more the thing occupies our attention, and the more likely we are to fall. Every wrestler knows that the harder you grip your opponent, the more firmly he grips you. The new response is to turn. Not to fight the sin, but to look away from it to Christ, and to hold the fact: I died. The person to whom this appeal is being made no longer legally exists. I am not obliged to answer.

Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, that ye should obey it in the lusts thereof. ROMANS 6:12

Observe that Paul does not say sin is dead. Sin is very much alive; that is why he tells us not to let it reign. What has died is not sin but us. Sin remains as a power in the world and a pull in the body, but its legal claim upon us has been dissolved by death, because he that is dead is freed from sin (Romans 6:7). A creditor may shout as loudly as he likes at the grave of a debtor. The debt is uncollectable.

When we fail

What of the times we reckon and fall anyway? Nee’s counsel here was full of common sense and free of condemnation. Failure does not disprove the fact. If a man falls out of a chair, the chair still exists. When we fail, we do not go back to the beginning. We confess, receive cleansing by the blood — if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9) — and we return to the same ground. The ground has not shifted. Our standing was never established by our success in standing.

Nee summed the matter up in a sentence that recurs in various forms across his ministry: it is not our reckoning that makes the thing true; it is because the thing is true that we may reckon. Faith adds nothing to the facts. It simply consents to them.

Fact, faith and feeling

Nee used a picture here which had been current among deeper-life teachers before him and which he made his own. It concerns the order of three things. Imagine three men walking along the top of a wall, in single file. The first is called Fact, the second Faith, and the third Feeling. So long as Faith keeps his eyes on Fact and walks steadily behind him, all three proceed safely, and Feeling follows without difficulty. But let Faith turn round to see how Feeling is getting on, and he loses sight of Fact — and Faith and Feeling both come off the wall together. The point is about direction of gaze. Faith looks at fact. It does not look at feeling, and it certainly does not depend on it. This is worth pressing, because the ordinary Christian instinct is exactly the reverse. We wake, we consult our sense of God’s nearness, and we conclude from it whether things are well with us. On a morning when we feel warm towards God we believe we are in fellowship; on a flat morning we assume something is wrong. fields.title: Present
fields.body_html:
Yield yourselves unto God, as those that are alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness unto God. ROMANS 6:13

The third word is present, or as the Authorised Version has it, yield. Here the teaching turns from what God has done to what the believer must decide. Nee was insistent about the order. Consecration comes after knowing and reckoning, not before. This runs against the grain of a great deal of preaching, which begins with the appeal for surrender and applies it to people who have no idea what they are surrendering or on what basis. The result is a familiar and demoralising pattern: an emotional response at a meeting, a genuine intention, a few weeks of effort, and then a return to the old life with an added sense of failure. Why does it fail? Because the man is offering to God something God has already condemned. He is presenting the old man for service. And God has no use for Adam, however sincerely Adam offers himself.

Consecration is a response to a fact

The consecration Romans 6 asks for is offered by a particular sort of person: as those that are alive from the dead. Not those trying to die. Those who have died and been raised.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

By the mercies of God. Paul spends eleven chapters describing what God has done before he asks for anything. The appeal rests upon the argument. Nee drew a straight line here: consecration is never the price of blessing; it is the response to blessing already received. He put it in terms of ownership. If a man buys a house, the house is his by right of purchase, whether or not the previous occupant hands over the keys. But until the keys are handed over, the owner cannot use what belongs to him. Consecration is the handing over of keys to a Proprietor who has already paid.

What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price. 1 CORINTHIANS 6:19–20

Ye are not your own. It is not a request for a loan. It is notice of a change of ownership that has already occurred.

Once for all, and then daily

There is a paradox in Nee’s treatment which he never tried to resolve, because Scripture does not resolve it either. Consecration is a definite act, and it is also a continual condition. The definite act matters. He often urged believers to a decisive transaction with God — a particular day, a particular prayer, a line drawn — and he observed that many believers drift for years precisely because they have never made one. The Levites were consecrated on a specific day. The burnt offering was laid on the altar at a specific hour. But the offering laid on the altar was also, in the nature of things, consumed daily. So Paul speaks of a living sacrifice — a phrase which, as generations of preachers have noticed, contains its own difficulty, since a living sacrifice may always climb down off the altar. Nee’s counsel was to make the transaction once and then to maintain it by successive small obediences. The great surrender is settled in a moment. It is worked out in the question of what you do with an evening, a grudge, a sum of money, an ambition.

The members

Note the specificity of the text. Paul does not ask for a vague spiritual dedication. He asks for the members — the actual parts of the actual body — to be handed over as instruments. Nee took this concretely. The tongue is a member; is it an instrument of righteousness or of sin? The eyes are members. The hands, the feet, the ears. The mind. The money, which is the stored labour of the hands. Consecration that never reaches the members is a sentiment, not a sacrifice. In the Kuling trainings of 1948 and 1949 he pressed this to its practical conclusion, calling believers to hand over their possessions, homes and livelihoods to the Lord’s disposal. Many did, at real cost. Whatever one makes of the particular form that movement took, the principle behind it is unarguably apostolic: a Lord who owns you owns your things.

One last word, and it is a liberating one. God does not ask us to make ourselves useful before He will accept the offering. The altar sanctifies the gift, not the reverse. Bring what you are, not what you hope to become.

When God asks for Isaac

Consecration is easy in general and difficult in particular. Nee knew this, and he returned repeatedly to the moment where the general becomes particular.

Take now thy son, thine only son Isaac, whom thou lovest, and get thee into the land of Moriah; and offer him there for a burnt offering. GENESIS 22:2

He drew out something about this demand that is easy to miss and, once seen, hard to forget. Isaac was not Abraham’s achievement. Isaac was God’s own gift — the promised son, born to a couple long past hope, the very pledge of everything God had covenanted. And it was this, precisely this, that God asked for back. Nee’s application, developed at length in Changed into His Likeness, was that God frequently requires from us the thing He Himself gave. Not our sins, which we should be glad to surrender, but our blessings. The ministry He raised up. The child. The health. The work into which we poured thirty years. Why? Because a gift can take the place of the Giver, and it usually does. What Abraham was being asked to give up was not a boy; it was a dependence that had attached itself to the promise rather than to the One who promised. This is where consecration is actually tested. Most of us are willing enough for God to have our failures. The question is whether He may have the one thing we have quietly decided He may not ask for — and every honest believer knows what that thing is, usually within a few seconds of being asked. Nee added an observation of great pastoral value. Abraham received Isaac back. The knife was raised and the hand was stopped, and what came down the mountain was a father and a son who now belonged to God rather than to each other. In most cases, he said, God does not take the thing; He takes our grip on it. But He will not settle for less than the raised knife, because a surrender with conditions attached is not a surrender.

Now I know that thou fearest God, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son from me. GENESIS 22:12

Now I know. Something was established on that mountain that could not have been established anywhere else.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you have never made a definite transaction of consecration with God, make one. Set a date. Write it down. Tell someone. 2. Go through your members one by one — eyes, tongue, hands, mind, time, money — and name for each a specific way it is currently an instrument of unrighteousness. Present each one deliberately. 3. Check the foundation. Are you consecrating in order to gain God’s favour, or because you already have it? Only the second will last. 4. Identify one thing you are holding that is not yours: a resentment, a possession, a plan for your life. Hand over the keys. 5. Ask God to show you tomorrow’s small obedience, and do that one thing rather than making a large new resolution.

A PRAYER
Father, You have bought me. I did not set the price and I cannot revoke the sale. I am not my own.
I have kept back rooms in a house that belongs to You. Today I hand over the keys — not to earn anything, for You have already given me everything, but because it is Yours and I have been withholding it.
Take my body. Take my tongue, my eyes, my hands, my hours, my money, my ambitions. I lay them on Your altar, and I ask You to keep them there when I am tempted to climb down. Amen.

fields.title: The Spirit of Life
fields.body_html:
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. ROMANS 8:2

Romans 7 is the most uncomfortable chapter in the Bible for anyone who has ever tried to be good. Here is a man who wants what is right, who delights in the law of God after the inward man, who hates what he does — and who cannot do the thing he wants. He is not a rebel. He is a sincere, earnest, thoroughly defeated believer. And Nee made much of the fact that the chapter is dense with the first person singular. Count the times I, me and my occur in those verses; it is a great many. That, he said, is the whole problem in a single grammatical observation. Romans 7 is the biography of a Christian trying to serve God by himself.

For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not. ROMANS 7:18

Nee observed something that is easy to miss. The great discovery of Romans 7 is not that I am a sinner — the man knew that already. It is that I am helpless. And God allows the experience of chapter seven precisely in order to bring us to the end of our own resources, because until a man knows he cannot, he will not stop trying.

Two laws, and how one defeats the other

The way out is not more effort. It is another law. The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus hath made me free from the law of sin and death. Nee used the illustration of gravity. A stone falls because of a law; you cannot argue with it, and you cannot suspend it by resolution. But a bird rises, because a higher law — the law of life — is at work in it. The law of gravity has not been repealed. It has been overcome by something stronger. So deliverance is not the removal of the flesh, nor the improvement of the will. It is the operation of a life that is not ours.

Two aspects of one Spirit

Here Nee introduced a distinction he considered vital, and which he treated at length in The Normal Christian Life and in The Communion of the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit is given to the believer in two aspects.

There is the Spirit within — the indwelling Spirit, given to every believer at the new birth, whose work is life, transformation and the production of Christ’s character.

Now if any man have not the Spirit of Christ, he is none of his. ROMANS 8:9

And there is the Spirit upon — the outpoured Spirit, whose work is power and equipment for service and testimony.

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me. ACTS 1:8

The two are not the same, Nee argued, and confusing them causes real damage in both directions. Some believers seek power when what they need is life, and become noisy and fruitless. Others, having tasted the inward work, despise the outward and remain ineffective in service. He was careful, though, about how the second is obtained. It is not a reward for spiritual attainment, and it is not extracted from God by fasting or pleading. It is, like everything else in his teaching, already given, and to be received. The Spirit was poured out at Pentecost upon the whole Body; the individual believer does not ask God to do it again but takes his share in what has been done.

Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear. ACTS 2:33

The condition

If the Spirit’s fullness is not earned, is there any condition at all? Nee answered that there is one, and it is not spiritual excellence. It is obedience.

And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him. ACTS 5:32

The Spirit is not given to the worthy but to the willing. And because the Spirit is a Person and not a force, the practical question of the Christian life is not how to use Him but how not to grieve Him.

And grieve not the holy Spirit of God, whereby ye are sealed unto the day of redemption. EPHESIANS 4:30

Nee taught believers to attend to the inward sense — that quiet checking, that absence of peace, which is the Spirit’s ordinary way of guiding a consecrated heart. Not a voice, not a sign, not a hunch dignified with religious language, but a settled inward witness that either presses forward or holds back. Learning to obey that check in small matters is, he said, the whole training of the spiritual life.

A word of balance. Because Nee spoke of an inward sense, some readers have made subjective impressions into an authority that overrides Scripture. That is a serious error, and it is not his. The Spirit who speaks within is the same Spirit who wrote the Word, and He does not contradict Himself. Where the inward sense and the plain teaching of Scripture appear to disagree, Scripture governs — every time, without exception.

Flesh and Spirit, day by day

Romans 8 describes the position. Galatians 5 describes the daily experience of it, and Nee treated the two together.

This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other. GALATIANS 5:16–17

Two things in that passage governed his teaching. First, the conflict is normal. A believer who finds two contrary pulls within him is not thereby unspiritual; he is thereby alive. The unregenerate man has no such civil war, because there is only one party in the field. The presence of the struggle is evidence of the Spirit’s arrival, not of His absence. Second — and this is the practical point — the command is not fight the flesh. It is walk in the Spirit, with the promise attached that the other thing will not then be fulfilled. The negative is achieved by the positive. Nee compared it to a room full of stale air. You may attempt to remove the darkness with a shovel, or you may open the shutters. Light does not have to fight darkness; it only has to be admitted. This reframes the whole business of temptation. The question in the moment is not how do I suppress this? but what does walking in the Spirit look like in the next five minutes? Sometimes the answer is prayer. Often it is something quite unspiritual-looking: doing the next duty, leaving the room, telephoning a brother, going to bed. He drew the same conclusion about Christian character. The virtues of Galatians 5:22–23 are called fruit, not achievements, and fruit is grown rather than manufactured. Nobody produces patience by resolving to be patient; the tree produces it, given root, light and time.

But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. GALATIANS 5:22–23

Note that it is fruit, singular, with nine descriptions — one life expressing itself in nine directions. You do not select among them. Where the life is present, the whole cluster eventually appears.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Count the personal pronouns in Romans 7:14–25 for yourself. Ask whether your own prayers sound more like Romans 7 or Romans 8. 2. Have you come to the end of trying? If not, ask God to bring you there; it is a mercy, not a punishment. 3. Distinguish in your own experience between needing life and needing power. Which have you been seeking, and which do you actually lack? 4. Practise obeying the inward check this week in one small matter — a word not spoken, a purchase not made. Small obediences train the ear. 5. Test every inward impression against Scripture. Where the two conflict, submit to the Word without negotiation.

A PRAYER
Holy Spirit, I have tried to live the Christian life with my own strength and I have failed exactly as Scripture said I would. I am not merely guilty; I am helpless. I confess it.
Be in me the law of life that overcomes the law of sin. Do in me what I cannot do for myself.
And clothe me with what I need for service, not because I deserve it, but because Christ has been exalted and has poured it out. Make me quick to obey Your least restraint, and keep me from grieving You today. Amen.

Learning to obey that check in small matters is, he said, the whole training of the spiritual life. A word of balance. Galatians 5 describes the daily experience of it, and Nee treated the two together. This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other. GALATIANS 5:16–17 Two things in that passage governed his teaching. The unregenerate man has no such civil war, because there is only one party in the field. The presence of the struggle is evidence of the Spirit’s arrival, not of His absence. Second — and this is the practical point — the command is not fight the flesh. It is walk in the Spirit, with the promise attached that the other thing will not then be fulfilled. The negative is achieved by the positive. Nee compared it to a room full of stale air. You may attempt to remove the darkness with a shovel, or you may open the shutters. Light does not have to fight darkness; it only has to be admitted. This reframes the whole business of temptation. The question in the moment is not how do I suppress this? but what does walking in the Spirit look like in the next five minutes? Sometimes the answer is prayer. Often it is something quite unspiritual-looking: doing the next duty, leaving the room, telephoning a brother, going to bed. He drew the same conclusion about Christian character. The virtues of Galatians 5:22–23 are called fruit, not achievements, and fruit is grown rather than manufactured. Nobody produces patience by resolving to be patient; the tree produces it, given root, light and time. But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. GALATIANS 5:22–23 Note that it is fruit, singular, with nine descriptions — one life expressing itself in nine directions. You do not select among them. Where the life is present, the whole cluster eventually appears. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Count the personal pronouns in Romans 7:14–25 for yourself. Ask whether your own prayers sound more like Romans 7 or Romans 8. 2. Have you come to the end of trying? If not, ask God to bring you there; it is a mercy, not a punishment. 3. Distinguish in your own experience between needing life and needing power. Which have you been seeking, and which do you actually lack? 4. Practise obeying the inward check this week in one small matter — a word not spoken, a purchase not made. Small obediences train the ear. 5. Test every inward impression against Scripture. Where the two conflict, submit to the Word without negotiation. A PRAYER Holy Spirit, I have tried to live the Christian life with my own strength and I have failed exactly as Scripture said I would. I am not merely guilty; I am helpless. I confess it. Be in me the law of life that overcomes the law of sin. Do in me what I cannot do for myself. And clothe me with what I need for service, not because I deserve it, but because Christ has been exalted and has poured it out. Make me quick to obey Your least restraint, and keep me from grieving You today. Amen.

fields.title: Sit
fields.body_html:
And hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus. EPHESIANS 2:6

Among all Nee’s books, the shortest is arguably the most perfectly constructed. Sit, Walk, Stand takes the letter to the Ephesians and finds in it three words that mark its three movements: our position before God, our life in the world, and our attitude towards the enemy. And the order is not negotiable. Everything hangs on beginning in the right place.

Christianity begins with a chair

The natural religious instinct is to begin with walking — with conduct, effort, duty. Nee’s contention is that the Christian life begins with sitting down.

Even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ, (by grace ye are saved;) and hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus. EPHESIANS 2:5–6

Sitting, he pointed out, is the posture of one whose work is done. We do not sit down to a task; we sit down after it. And the striking thing about Ephesians 2 is that the sitting has already happened, and it happened to people who were at the time dead in sins and contributed precisely nothing to it. He drew out a comparison with creation. Man was made on the sixth day and his first full day of existence was the seventh — the day of God’s rest. Man did not work six days and then rest; he began in a rest that God had already entered. So the believer begins his Christian life at the point of God’s completed work, not at the beginning of his own.

There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God. For he that is entered into his rest, he also hath ceased from his own works, as God did from his. HEBREWS 4:9–10

Not resting from work, but working from rest

Nee was quick to guard the point against the obvious misreading. To sit is not to be idle. The Christian works — Ephesians itself is full of instruction about conduct, family, labour and warfare. The question is not whether we work but where the work starts.

The difference is between working towards a position and working from one. A man who is trying to earn his acceptance labours under an anxiety that never lifts, because there is always more to do. A man who has been seated labours out of a security he did not create and cannot lose. He was fond of the picture of a man on a boat. If he tries to push the boat along, he exhausts himself and it barely moves. If he sits down and lets the current carry him, he arrives. The strength required to be carried is nil, but one must actually sit.

The gift and the giving up

There is a cost to sitting, and Nee did not hide it. It is the cost of abandoning the satisfaction of having contributed. We would rather help. There is something in every one of us — and it is the oldest thing in us — that would prefer a salvation we had a hand in. To sit down is to admit that the whole thing was done without us, and there is a humbling in that which many believers avoid for years by staying busy.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

Where the chair is

One more detail Nee would not let pass: in heavenly places. The believer’s seat is not on earth. It is above — in the place where Christ is, at the right hand of God, far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion (Ephesians 1:21). This matters enormously for what comes later. The Christian does not fight his way up to victory; he views the battle from above it. He does not struggle to reach a place of authority; he is already seated with the One who has it. Every question of warfare in chapter six will be settled by what was established in chapter two.

Sit is the first word, and it is the one that most of us skip. If your Christian life is marked by chronic tiredness — not the honest tiredness of labour, but the grey exhaustion of never having arrived — the problem is almost certainly here. You have been walking without having sat down.

Martha’s kitchen

Nee was fond of the scene at Bethany, and used it to make a distinction that cuts across most of our assumptions about Christian service.

But Martha was cumbered about much serving …But one thing is needful: and Mary hath chosen that good part, which shall not be taken away from her. LUKE 10:40, 42

The striking thing, he observed, is that Martha was not doing anything wrong. She was serving Jesus. The meal needed cooking; somebody had to cook it; the guest was the Son of God and the hospitality was genuine. If we are honest, most of us would rather have Martha in our congregation than Mary. What was wrong was not the work but its source. Martha was cumbered — the word suggests being dragged about, pulled in several directions. And the symptom appeared, as it always does, in her speech: she complained about her sister, and she reproached the Lord for not noticing. Service that comes out of restlessness reliably produces resentment towards those who are not serving. Nee’s application was uncomfortable for active people. A great deal of Christian work, he said, is Martha’s work: undertaken for the Lord, but not out of rest, and therefore carrying an undertone of strain, comparison and self-justification that everyone around can feel. The alternative is not idleness. Mary is not commended for being lazy; she is commended for having chosen the one needful thing, and the order matters. Elsewhere in the Gospels Mary of Bethany is the one who anoints the Lord for His burial — an act of service so costly that it was criticised, and so perceptive that He defended it. The woman who sat became the woman who understood, and the woman who understood gave the most. Sitting, in other words, does not reduce service. It changes where service comes from, and it changes what service is worth.

It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep. PSALM 127:2

Nee’s test was simple, and it is worth applying honestly. Does your service leave you resenting the people who are not doing it? If so, the problem is probably not their idleness. It is the place your own labour is starting from.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself plainly: am I working towards God’s acceptance or from it? Your answer will show in how you feel after a day of failure. 2. Take Ephesians 1 and 2 and mark every verb whose subject is God. Notice how few of them have you as the subject. 3. Name one activity in your ministry or service that you are doing out of anxiety rather than rest. Consider whether God asked for it. 4. Practise a deliberate sitting: take fifteen minutes to receive rather than to petition. Say nothing. Simply consent to what has been done. 5. Where you are facing opposition, remind yourself where your seat is — above it, not beneath it.

A PRAYER
Lord, I have been trying to reach a place You have already given me. I have been labouring towards a rest You entered without my help.
Forgive the pride that would rather assist than receive. I lay down the satisfaction of having contributed.
Teach me to sit — not in idleness, but in the finished work of Christ. And from that seat, let all my labour begin. Amen.

fields.title: Walk
fields.body_html:
I therefore, the prisoner of the Lord, beseech you that ye walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called. EPHESIANS 4:1

The letter turns at chapter four. Having spent three chapters describing what God has done, Paul says therefore — and for the next two chapters he deals with conduct. Nee’s point about this hinge is simple and important: the therefore is load-bearing. Christian behaviour is not a set of requirements imposed upon us in order to make us acceptable. It is the appropriate outworking of a position already occupied. We do not walk in order to sit. We walk because we are seated.

Worthy of a calling, not worthy of a wage

Note the phrase: walk worthy of the vocation wherewith ye are called. Not worthy of God — no one is. Worthy of the calling. There is a fittingness being asked for, the way a man’s clothing should suit the occasion he has been invited to.

That ye put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts; and be renewed in the spirit of your mind; and that ye put on the new man, which after God is created in righteousness and true holiness. EPHESIANS 4:22–24

Nee laid weight on the metaphor of clothing. Putting off and putting on are not the same as killing and creating. The old man was crucified — that was settled at the cross and is not repeated. What we do daily is decline to wear him. The garment is discarded, not the corpse reexecuted. This distinction saved a great many of his hearers from a wearying spiritual practice in which every day begins with an attempt to die all over again. The death is behind us. The wardrobe choice is in front of us.

The walk is with others

There is something easily overlooked in Ephesians 4 to 6 which Nee never overlooked: almost every instruction concerns another person. Lying is forbidden because we are members one of another (Ephesians 4:25). Anger must not be carried overnight. Stealing is replaced by working so that there may be something to give away. Corrupt speech is replaced by speech that builds up the hearer. Bitterness, wrath, clamour and evil speaking are to be put away, and in their place: be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ’s sake hath forgiven you (Ephesians 4:32). Then follow the household relationships — husbands and wives, parents and children, servants and masters. Nee found this deeply significant. The deeper life is not tested in the prayer closet, where no one contradicts us. It is tested at the table, in the marriage, in the workshop, in the way a man speaks to those who cannot answer him back. He had little patience for spirituality that flourished in meetings and collapsed at home. The measure of a man’s walk, he taught, is taken by the people who live with him.

Walking in love, in light, and carefully

Ephesians 5 gives the walk three qualities, and Nee treated them in turn. Walk in love (5:2) — and the standard given is Christ’s self-giving, not our natural affection. Love here is measured by what it costs, not by what it feels. Walk as children of light (5:8) — which chiefly means transparency. The believer has nothing to hide, and the willingness to be known is itself a form of holiness. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light (5:13). Walk circumspectly (5:15) — literally, accurately; walking as a man does who is picking his way across broken ground. Nee connected this to the redeeming of time: because the days are evil (5:16). A short life in a dark age is not to be spent carelessly.

And through all of it, the enabling is the same as the beginning. Be filled with the Spirit (5:18) stands in the middle of these instructions, not as one more command among many, but as the power by which the rest become possible. Nee’s whole point is that Christian conduct is Christ’s life reaching the surface. Where it is anything else — willpower, temperament, culture, fear of what people will say — it may look similar for a while, but it will not hold.

The renewing of the mind

Between the position and the walk, Paul places one more thing, and Nee would not let it be skipped.

And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God. ROMANS 12:2

Conformity, he pointed out, happens by default. It requires no decision. A body placed in a mould takes the shape of the mould simply by remaining there, and a believer immersed in the assumptions of his age will absorb them without ever consciously adopting one of them. The world does not usually argue us out of our convictions. It simply makes certain things unthinkable and other things obvious, and we adjust. Transformation, by contrast, works in the opposite direction — from within outwards — and it operates through the mind. This is why Nee gave such weight to the sustained reading of Scripture. Not reading for sermon material, and not reading to complete a schedule, but the slow saturation by which a man’s instinctive judgements begin to change. The renewed mind is not merely a mind with more information in it. It is a mind that has come to find different things obvious.

And be renewed in the spirit of your mind. EPHESIANS 4:23

He noted the practical outcome Paul attaches to it: that ye may prove what is …the will of God. Guidance, on this understanding, is far less often a matter of special direction than of a mind so shaped by God that it recognises His will when it appears. The believer who is forever asking for signs may be revealing that the ordinary means have been neglected. There is a test in this that anyone can apply. Take an area where the culture around you holds a settled opinion — about money, about status, about forgiveness, about who deserves respect. Ask what Scripture says. Then ask which of the two your gut agrees with. The gap between them is the measure of how much renewing remains to be done. Nee’s expectation was that this work is gradual and mostly invisible, and that it shows up not in what we say we believe but in what we do without thinking.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask the people you live with, not the people you minister to, how your walk is going. Their answer is the accurate one. 2. Identify one garment of the old man you have kept in the wardrobe — a habit of speech, a way of handling conflict. Take it off deliberately today rather than trying to die again. 3. Take Ephesians 4:25–32 and find the one command you break most often. Confess it as an offence against the Body, which is how Paul frames it.

4. Examine your speech for one week with a single question: did that build up the person who heard it? 5. Where are you walking carelessly with your time? Name one specific redemption of an hour, and make it this week.

A PRAYER
Father, You have seated me in Christ, and now You ask me to walk in a manner that suits it. I confess how often my conduct has contradicted my position.
Let my holiness be tested where it counts — in my home, with my family, among those who can do nothing for me. Guard my tongue. Take the bitterness out of me before the sun goes down.
I cannot produce this by resolve. Fill me with Your Spirit, and let Your own life come to the surface in the ordinary hours of this day. Amen.

The believer who is forever asking for signs may be revealing that the ordinary means have been neglected. There is a test in this that anyone can apply. Take an area where the culture around you holds a settled opinion — about money, about status, about forgiveness, about who deserves respect. Ask what Scripture says. Then ask which of the two your gut agrees with. The gap between them is the measure of how much renewing remains to be done. Nee’s expectation was that this work is gradual and mostly invisible, and that it shows up not in what we say we believe but in what we do without thinking. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Ask the people you live with, not the people you minister to, how your walk is going. Their answer is the accurate one. 2. Identify one garment of the old man you have kept in the wardrobe — a habit of speech, a way of handling conflict. Take it off deliberately today rather than trying to die again. 3. Take Ephesians 4:25–32 and find the one command you break most often. Confess it as an offence against the Body, which is how Paul frames it. 4. Examine your speech for one week with a single question: did that build up the person who heard it? 5. Where are you walking carelessly with your time?
