fields.title: Stand
fields.body_html:
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. EPHESIANS 6:13

The third movement of Ephesians is warfare, and Nee’s treatment of it in Sit, Walk, Stand turns on a single observation about the vocabulary. Paul does not tell us to attack. He does not tell us to advance, to storm, to conquer or to take ground. Four times in a few verses he uses one word: stand. Withstand, and having done all, stand. Stand therefore. Having done all, stand. You do not tell a soldier to hold his position unless the position is already his.

Fighting from victory, not for it

This is the whole of Nee’s doctrine of warfare, and it is simply chapter two applied to chapter six. The believer is seated with Christ far above all principality, and power, and might, and dominion (Ephesians 1:21). The battle was fought and settled at the cross and the resurrection.

And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it. COLOSSIANS 2:15

Having spoiled. Past. Finished. The enemy is a defeated enemy. What remains is not a war to be won but a victory to be maintained against a foe who does not accept the result. Nee’s practical conclusion follows: the Christian never prays for victory. He prays from it. To ask God to defeat the devil is, in his blunt phrasing, to ask God to do again what He has already done, and it betrays that we have not yet believed the report of the first battle.

The enemy’s chief weapon is a lie

If the ground is already ours, how does the enemy take it back? By persuading us that it is not. Nee identified the primary battlefield as the mind, and pointed to the armour itself as evidence. The helmet is salvation — protection for the head, the place of thought. The shield of faith quenches the fiery darts of the wicked (Ephesians 6:16), which are precisely injected thoughts: suggestions of doubt, accusation, despair, suspicion of God and of one another.

Casting down imaginations, and every high thing that exalteth itself against the knowledge of God, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ. 2 CORINTHIANS 10:5

He taught believers to recognise thoughts that do not originate with them. A sudden, alien, insistent accusation — God has abandoned you, you are finished, that brother despises you — may not be a conviction from the Spirit at all. Nee’s test was characteristically simple: the Holy Spirit convicts of specific sin in order to bring us to the cross, and His conviction leaves us with hope and a way forward. The accuser condemns the person in general terms and leaves us with despair and no way forward. Learn the difference and half the battle is over.

The armour is a Person

Nee also noted that every piece of the armour is elsewhere in Scripture attributed to Christ Himself. He is our righteousness, our peace, our salvation, our truth. To put on the armour is not to acquire seven spiritual accessories. It is to put on Christ.

But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh, to fulfil the lusts thereof. ROMANS 13:14

And note what is left unprotected. There is no armour for the back. The soldier who turns to flee is defenceless, which is another way of saying the same thing: the only safety is in standing.

The place of prayer

The passage ends not with a weapon but with a posture: praying always with all prayer and supplication in the Spirit (Ephesians 6:18). Nee took this as the point at which the armour is actually worn. Doctrine about warfare that does not issue in prayer is theory. The church that argues about spiritual authority and does not pray has none.

A caution, since this territory attracts excess. Nee’s own emphasis is remarkably sober. He does not encourage believers to seek out confrontations with evil powers, to catalogue them, or to make the enemy a preoccupation. Elsewhere he warned that undue attention to Satan is itself a victory for Satan, and that the safest Christian is the one occupied with Christ. Stand your ground, resist when resisted, and keep your eyes on the Lord.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. JAMES 4:7

Submission comes first in that verse. It always does.

Giving place

If the enemy’s claim is illegitimate, how does he obtain a foothold in the life of a believer at all? Paul answers in a passage Nee cited frequently, and the answer is startling in its ordinariness.

Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil. EPHESIANS 4:26–27

Give place. The word suggests granting ground, allowing an opening. And the context is not occultism, nor gross immorality, nor anything a congregation would recognise as dramatic. It is a quarrel carried overnight. Nee’s conclusion was that the enemy’s ordinary access to a Christian is through unforgiveness. Not through curses or rituals, but through resentment that has been kept, justified and nursed — usually with excellent reasons, since the grievance is generally real. He connected this to the Lord’s own warning at the end of the parable of the unforgiving servant, and to the clause in the prayer He taught us, which is the only petition He returned to afterwards and explained.

For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: but if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses. MATTHEW 6:14–15

The practical counsel was direct. Where you have been standing without result — praying, resisting, and finding no ground gained — look first for something you are holding. Not something being done to you, but something you are keeping. Forgiveness, he taught, is not a feeling to be waited for but a decision to be made and then maintained, frequently against the feelings, sometimes for years. He was careful to distinguish forgiveness from three things it is often confused with. It is not saying the wrong did not matter. It is not the restoration of trust, which must be earned. And it is not the removal of consequences, which may rightly continue. It is the surrender of one’s claim to repayment — handing the debt over to God, who alone can settle it justly.

Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves …for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord. ROMANS 12:19

The ground closes the moment the claim is released.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Change the grammar of your praying. Instead of asking God for victory, thank Him for the victory Christ has already won, and hold your ground. 2. Learn to distinguish conviction from accusation. Write the two tests down and keep them where you pray. 3. When an alien thought arrives, do not argue with it and do not accept it. Answer it with a specific verse and move on. 4. Check whether you have turned your back on any ground — a relationship, a besetting sin, a calling — because standing became costly. Return and stand. 5. Do not study the enemy. Study Christ. Notice this week how much of your attention each receives.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You met the enemy at the cross and You triumphed openly. I did not help, and I cannot improve upon it.
Forgive me for praying as though the outcome were still in doubt. Teach me to stand on ground You purchased with Your blood.
Guard my mind today. When accusation comes disguised as conviction, give me discernment. When the darts come, let faith be my shield. And keep me looking at You, not at him. Amen.

fields.title: Spirit, Soul and Body
fields.body_html:
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:23

In 1928, gravely ill with tuberculosis and expecting to die, Watchman Nee published his first substantial work. The Spiritual Man runs to three volumes and sets out an anatomy of the inner life that shaped everything he afterwards taught. Its central proposition is that man is not two parts but three.

The threefold constitution

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit, and of the joints and marrow. HEBREWS 4:12

Nee read Paul’s benediction in 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and this verse in Hebrews as teaching a real distinction between spirit and soul. The body is that by which we relate to the physical world. The soul is the seat of personality — mind, emotion and will; it is what makes a man himself, and it is by the soul that he relates to other people and to his own inner world. The spirit is the innermost part, by which alone a man relates to God. He found the pattern in Genesis: the Lord God formed man of the dust of the ground — the body; and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life — the spirit; and man became a living soul — the personality produced by the union of the two (Genesis 2:7). At the fall, he argued, the spirit died in the sense that it lost its communication with God, and man became soul-governed — ruled by his own mind, feelings and will rather than by God through the spirit. Regeneration is precisely the quickening of the spirit.

That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. JOHN 3:6

Why the distinction matters practically

One might think this a piece of technical anthropology of no use to an ordinary believer. Nee thought otherwise, and his reason is worth understanding.

If a man cannot tell the difference between what rises from his soul and what comes from his spirit, he will confuse emotion with the presence of God, mental clarity with revelation, and strength of will with faith. He will conclude he has been near to God because he was moved, and that God has departed because he feels flat.

But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:14

The word rendered natural there is, in the Greek, the soulish man — the man whose life is governed by the soul. Nee’s contention is that a genuine believer may nonetheless live a soulish Christian life: sincere, active, emotional, intelligent, and yet not walking by the Spirit at all. The remedy is discernment, and the instrument of discernment is the Word of God, which pierces to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit. Only Scripture can make that cut. We cannot make it ourselves by introspection — indeed introspection is a soulish activity and tends to deepen the problem.

Handle with care

Honesty requires a caution here, and Nee himself supplied part of it. Not all Bible teachers accept the trichotomy. Many careful expositors hold that Scripture uses spirit and soul largely interchangeably, that the Hebrews 4:12 passage speaks of the depth of the Word’s penetration rather than of a clean anatomical line, and that man is best understood as a unity viewed from different angles. That position is held by godly and serious readers of Scripture, and a believer who takes it loses nothing essential. Nee later grew uneasy about the systematising in The Spiritual Man. He is reported to have regretted the analytical thoroughness of it, on the grounds that readers were turning a description of spiritual experience into a technique for self-examination — which is exactly the soulishness the book was written to expose. That is the right way to hold this chapter. Take the pastoral insight, which is genuine and valuable: much that passes for spirituality is merely refined human life, and we need God to show us the difference. Leave the elaborate diagrams alone. A believer preoccupied with locating the boundary between his soul and his spirit has already lost the plot.

Three functions of the human spirit

Within his account of the spirit, Nee distinguished three operations, and this part of The Spiritual Man has proved more durable than the anatomy itself. Whatever one concludes about trichotomy, these three are recognisable in Christian experience. The first is conscience, by which God registers His approval or disapproval within us. Nee held that conscience is not merely a socially formed sense of right and wrong but the place where the Spirit speaks most directly and most unavoidably.

Which shew the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience also bearing witness. ROMANS 2:15

He taught believers to keep the conscience extremely tender, and warned that a conscience repeatedly overruled becomes progressively silent — having their conscience seared with a hot iron (1 Timothy 4:2). A believer who has learned to argue with his conscience has disabled his most reliable instrument. The second is intuition, by which he meant direct spiritual knowing that does not arrive by reasoning. This is the inward sense that something is right or wrong before one can say why. Nee grounded it in the Spirit’s witness:

The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God. ROMANS 8:16

Assurance of salvation, he pointed out, is precisely of this kind. No believer reasons his way to it, and no argument can finally remove it. The third is communion, or fellowship — the capacity by which we actually worship, as distinct from thinking about God or feeling moved by Him.

God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth. JOHN 4:24

The practical value of this threefold description is diagnostic. A believer can ask which faculty is engaged. Am I troubled in conscience, which requires confession or restitution? Do I have an intuitive check, which requires waiting? Or am I simply out of communion, which requires returning? Held as descriptions of experience rather than as a map of the soul’s architecture, they remain useful. Held as a system to be applied by introspection, they become the very soulishness Nee was warning against.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask honestly after your next moving worship service: was that God, or was that music? The question is not cynical. It is discernment.

2. Notice this week when you are drawing on mental cleverness or emotional energy in ministry rather than on God. Name one instance. 3. Let Scripture do the dividing. When you want to examine yourself, read the Word rather than turning inward. 4. Resist making a system of this. If you find yourself analysing your inner parts more than you are looking at Christ, stop. 5. Hold the doctrine loosely and the pastoral warning tightly. Be gracious with believers who read these texts differently.

A PRAYER
Father, I do not fully understand myself, and I have often mistaken my own feelings for Your presence and my own reasoning for Your voice.
Let Your Word do its work in me. Divide what is merely mine from what is truly Yours. I would rather be cut than deceived.
Keep me from turning this into a study of myself. Turn my eyes outward and upward, to Christ, in whom alone I am safe. Amen.

fields.title: The Breaking of the Outer Man
fields.body_html:
Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit. JOHN 12:24

If there is one book of Watchman Nee’s that his own generation of workers found most searching, it is the short volume published in English as The Release of the Spirit. Its argument can be stated in a sentence, and the sentence is uncomfortable. The believer’s greatest hindrance is not his weakness. It is his unbroken strength.

The alabaster box

Nee took his controlling image from Bethany.

And being in Bethany …there came a woman having an alabaster box of ointment of spikenard very precious; and she brake the box, and poured it on his head. MARK 14:3

The value was in the ointment, not the alabaster. But so long as the box remained whole, the fragrance stayed inside, and the house smelled of nothing at all. Only when the alabaster was broken did the perfume fill the room. So, Nee argued, with the believer. Christ dwells within by His Spirit — that is the treasure. But around that treasure is the outer man: our natural capability, our personality, our cleverness, our forcefulness, our charm, our opinions, our self-love. And the outer man does not automatically transmit the inner life. Frequently it imprisons it.

Nee made an observation about ministry which is easier to accept in principle than in practice.

An unbroken servant of God can be enormously impressive and spiritually sterile. His natural gifts are so strong that people meet the gift and never reach the Christ behind it. He gets in the way without ever intending to, and he is usually the last person to know. This is why, in Nee’s view, God’s central work in a servant is not the augmenting of his abilities but the reduction of his self-confidence.

How the breaking comes

And how does God do it? Not, Nee said, by our arrangement. We cannot break ourselves. Every attempt at self-imposed brokenness produces a new and subtler form of self-admiration — the man is now proud of his humility. God alone knows where the shell is thickest, and God alone can strike accurately. The instruments He uses are ordinary. A ministry that does not open as we expected. A rebuke we did not deserve, or one we did. A colleague who is promoted over us. Illness. Failure. The long, grinding disappointment of a work that never becomes what we envisioned. Nee’s counsel was to recognise the hand of God in these and to stop resisting.

The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise. PSALM 51:17

He drew attention to Jacob at Peniel — the man who wrestled and prevailed and went away limping for life. The limp was the blessing. The strong man had at last met Someone stronger, and the name he was given afterwards belonged to the crippled man, not the wrestler.

Broken, not destroyed

An important balance. Breaking is not the annihilation of personality. The alabaster box is broken; the ointment is not. Peter after Pentecost is still recognisably Peter — bold, quick, impetuous by temperament — but the boldness now serves Christ instead of Peter. God does not want colourless servants. He wants servants whose distinctiveness has been brought under the cross so that it conveys Christ rather than obstructing Him.

There is no shortcut here, and Nee offered none. He simply asked his hearers to stop defending the shell. Most of us spend our lives protecting exactly what God is trying to break — our reputation, our right to be understood, our record of being right. To lay those down voluntarily is not to be broken; only God does that. But it is to cease fighting Him while He does it.

Receiving the discipline

Since we cannot break ourselves, the question becomes how to respond when God does it. Nee taught that everything depends on the attitude taken to the instrument.

My son, despise not thou the chastening of the Lord, nor faint when thou art rebuked of him. HEBREWS 12:5

Two failures are named there, and Nee treated them as the two ditches on either side of the road. To despise the chastening is to refuse its meaning — to treat the difficulty as an accident, a mere administrative problem, an injustice to be resisted or a personality clash to be managed. The man does everything about his circumstances and nothing about himself. He may even succeed in escaping the situation, in which case God will generally arrange another. To faint is the opposite error: to be crushed, to conclude that God is against us, to give up. Nee had pastoral sympathy here, because the process is genuinely painful and often prolonged. But he insisted the two errors have the same root — both misread the hand behind the event.

Now no chastening for the present seemeth to be joyous, but grievous: nevertheless afterward it yieldeth the peaceable fruit of righteousness unto them which are exercised thereby. HEBREWS 12:11

He drew attention to the last clause. The fruit is not automatic; it belongs to those exercised thereby. Two men may pass through identical trouble; one emerges softened and the other hardened, and the difference lies in how each received it. Nee added two observations that have comforted many. First, God chooses the instrument, and He chooses accurately. The thing that breaks us is rarely the thing we would have picked, and is almost always the thing we most wished to avoid. That precision is not cruelty. It is evidence of attention. Second, God does not break more than is necessary, and He does not break carelessly. The purpose is release, not ruin. He is after the fragrance, not the destruction of the vessel.

The next time you are misunderstood, do not explain yourself. Let it stand for one day and watch what rises in you. 4. Stop protecting your reputation in one specific relationship this week. 5. Ask a trusted friend where your personality gets in the way of your ministry. Do not defend the answer.

I cannot break myself, and if I tried I would only become proud of it. So I ask instead: do it Yourself, in Your own way, at Your own hour, and hold me steady when it hurts. Let there be less of me, so there may be more of You. Amen.

fields.title: The Latent Power of the Soul
fields.body_html:
Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God: because many false prophets are gone out into the world. 1 JOHN 4:1

We come now to the most contested thing Watchman Nee ever taught, and it would be dishonest to present his ministry without it. In 1933 he published a short book whose English title is The Latent Power of the Soul. It is brief, strange, and has caused more argument than anything else he wrote.

The argument

Nee began from the dominion given to Adam.

And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air, and over the cattle, and over all the earth. GENESIS 1:26

Adam, he reasoned, possessed capacities far beyond anything we now know — faculties of knowledge and mastery suited to the government of a whole creation. When he fell, God did not annihilate these powers. Instead they were shut up, buried, rendered dormant. The flesh became, in Nee’s phrase, a prison to the soul’s abilities. The powers remain, latent, in every descendant of Adam. And here is the point of the book: Satan works to release them. Occult phenomena — telepathy, second sight, hypnotic influence, the transmission of thought, powers displayed in heathen religion — are, on this reading, not necessarily the direct action of demons in every case, but the awakening of buried human soul-power under satanic direction. Nee’s warning was twofold. First, that a believer might unwittingly develop and use this soul-force in Christian work, mistaking it for the power of the Holy Spirit. Second, that in the last days such power would be released on a great scale to support the deception of Antichrist.

Even him, whose coming is after the working of Satan with all power and signs and lying wonders. 2 THESSALONIANS 2:9

His conclusion was that the believer’s soul-power must be kept under the cross — not developed, not cultivated, not released, but held in death, so that only the Holy Spirit operates through him.

What is genuinely valuable here

Strip away the speculative framework and a real pastoral concern remains, and it is one the New Testament shares. There is such a thing as spiritual power that is not from God. Scripture says so plainly. Pharaoh’s magicians duplicated some of Moses’ signs. Simon of Samaria had bewitched a city. The girl at Philippi brought her masters much gain by soothsaying, and what she said about Paul was perfectly accurate. The Lord Himself warned that many would come to Him having prophesied, cast out devils and done many wonderful works in His name, and would hear I never knew you (Matthew 7:22–23). Nee’s insistence that results do not validate a ministry is therefore thoroughly biblical, and badly needed in every generation. Crowds, healings, manifestations, influence over people, the ability to move an audience — none of these is self-authenticating. A man may be powerful and not be sent.

For such are false apostles, deceitful workers, transforming themselves into the apostles of Christ. And no marvel; for Satan himself is transformed into an angel of light. 2 CORINTHIANS 11:13–14

Equally sound is his warning about the preacher who has learned to work upon a congregation — who knows how to build the emotional pressure, when to drop the voice, how to produce a response. That is a real danger, and it is not less dangerous for being unconscious.

Where it must be questioned

Now the other side, and it must be said plainly, because a book that presented this teaching without qualification would be doing the reader harm. The theory of latent Adamic soul-power is not taught in Scripture. It is a construction, built by inference upon Genesis 1:26 and a handful of texts that do not naturally bear it, and it owes a good deal to nineteenth-century writers who were preoccupied with the occult — G. H. Pember and Jessie Penn-Lewis among them — whose works Nee absorbed through Margaret Barber’s library. The Bible nowhere describes Adam as possessing psychic faculties, nowhere says those faculties were made dormant, and nowhere identifies occult phenomena as their release. The practical dangers of the theory are considerable, and church history has demonstrated them. It supplies a mechanism for attributing to human soul-power any spiritual phenomenon one dislikes, which makes it an instrument for dismissing the genuine work of God without examining it. It can foster a chronic suspicion of one’s own faculties, so that a believer becomes afraid of his mind, his emotions and his imagination — all of which God made and intends to sanctify, not suppress. And it can breed a fearful, inward-looking spirituality that is preoccupied with hidden dangers rather than occupied with Christ. The apostolic method of testing is not a theory of soul-power. It is simpler and more reliable:

Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God. 1 JOHN 4:2
Ye shall know them by their fruits. MATTHEW 7:16

Doctrine about Christ, and fruit in the life. Those are the tests Scripture gives, and they are sufficient.

How then should this chapter be used? Take the warning and leave the theory. Refuse to be impressed by power as such. Test everything by the Word and by fruit. Be honest about the manipulative techniques available to anyone who speaks in public. But do not adopt a speculative anthropology that Scripture does not teach, and do not let fear of your own soul make you a timid, suspicious Christian. Nee himself would have said — has said, repeatedly, elsewhere — that the safest believer is the one whose attention is on the Lord.

What Scripture does say

Having questioned the theory, it would be a mistake to leave the reader with the impression that the New Testament is unconcerned about spiritual danger. It is very concerned, and it speaks about it clearly. The point is that what it actually says is both more sober and more encouraging than the framework built upon it. Scripture affirms that the conflict is real and that its adversaries are not merely human.

For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. EPHESIANS 6:12

It affirms that deception is the enemy’s principal method, and that believers should be alert to it — lest Satan should get an advantage of us: for we are not ignorant of his devices (2 Corinthians 2:11). And it affirms, with equal clarity, that the outcome is not in question, that the believer is not helpless, and that the indwelling Christ is greater than anything ranged against him.

Ye are of God, little children, and have overcome them: because greater is he that is in you, than he that is in the world. 1 JOHN 4:4

What Scripture does not do is invite us into detailed speculation about mechanisms. It gives no anatomy of how occult power operates. It supplies no taxonomy of spiritual forces for our study. The information it withholds is information we do not need, and the New Testament’s reticence on the subject is itself instructive. The apostolic pattern is therefore: be aware, be armed, be unimpressed by displays of power, and be occupied with Christ. Believers who follow that pattern are safe. Believers who become specialists in the workings of darkness frequently are not — they grow fearful, suspicious of other Christians, and strangely fascinated by the very thing they claim to oppose.

Finally, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are honest, whatsoever things are just, whatsoever things are pure …think on these things. PHILIPPIANS 4:8

That is Paul’s instruction about what to fill the mind with, given in a letter written from prison by a man who knew perfectly well that the powers of darkness were real.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Adopt the two apostolic tests as your settled practice: what does this teach about Christ, and what fruit does it produce over time? 2. Examine your own public ministry, if you have one, for techniques that work on people rather than serve them. Name one and abandon it. 3. Refuse to be moved by results alone — whether other people’s or your own. 4. Where you have been suspicious of a genuine work of God because it was unfamiliar, repent of it. 5. Do not become a hunter of counterfeits. Give more attention to knowing Christ than to identifying the false.

A PRAYER
Lord, I want to be discerning without becoming suspicious, and open without becoming gullible. I cannot manage either balance on my own.
Keep me from every power that is not Yours, including the power of my own personality over other people. Where I have learned to manipulate, forgive me and unteach me.
And keep me from fear. You did not give me a spirit of fear. Fix my attention on Christ, and let me test all things by Your Word. Amen.

fields.title: Authority and Submission
fields.body_html:
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. ROMANS 13:1

In the summers of 1948 and 1949, on Kuling Mountain near Foochow, Watchman Nee gathered the workers for what proved to be the last training of his life. The messages he gave there were afterwards published as Spiritual Authority, and they are among the most penetrating — and the most dangerous — things he ever said.

Authority is the first principle of the universe

Nee’s starting point was that the deepest issue in the universe is not sin but authority. Sin is a symptom. Rebellion is the disease. He traced it to the fall of Lucifer, in whom the first act of rebellion was a declaration of independence:

I will ascend into heaven, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God …I will be like the most High. ISAIAH 14:13–14

Five times I will. Nothing immoral is proposed. What is proposed is self-government. And that, Nee argued, is the essence of all sin: not chiefly the doing of wrong things, but the refusal to be under. The same pattern appears in Eden. The serpent’s offer was autonomy — ye shall be as gods (Genesis 3:5) — and the fruit was merely the mechanism. Against this stands the obedience of the Son.

And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. PHILIPPIANS 2:8

Christ, who was equal with God, took the position of submission and never once left it. That, in Nee’s teaching, is the restoration of the moral order of the universe.

Delegated authority

From this he drew his second point: God exercises His authority through delegates. Parents in the home. Elders in the church. Masters over servants. Rulers in the state. Husbands in the marriage. These are not merely convenient social arrangements; they are, in his view, appointments through which God governs, and how a man treats them reveals how he regards God. He took his examples chiefly from the Old Testament. Korah, Dathan and Abiram, who challenged Moses and were swallowed by the earth. Miriam, struck with leprosy for speaking against her brother. Ham, cursed through his son for exposing his father’s shame while his two brothers walked backwards with a garment. Above all David, who twice had Saul in his hand and would not touch him, though Saul was murderous, disobedient and already rejected by God — for who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord’s anointed, and be guiltless? (1 Samuel 26:9). David’s restraint is the model. The authority was corrupt; the office was still God’s. And David left the removal of Saul to God, which God duly accomplished without David’s help.

Submission and obedience are not the same

Here Nee made a distinction that saves the whole teaching from becoming monstrous, and it deserves emphasis. Obedience is a matter of conduct; submission is a matter of attitude. Obedience is conditional — there are commands a believer must not obey. Submission is unconditional in spirit, in the sense that we never adopt the posture of a rebel. But they did not revile the council, organise against it, or set themselves up as an alternative authority. They declined to obey, and they accepted the beating. That is submission without obedience, and Nee held it up as the pattern: where a delegated authority commands what God forbids, the believer must refuse — and must refuse in a spirit that is not rebellious, accepting whatever consequences follow.

A necessary and serious warning

This teaching has been abused, and any honest presentation of it must say so clearly. In some circles influenced by these messages — and in many others that never heard of Watchman Nee — the doctrine of delegated authority has been used to shield leaders from accountability, to silence legitimate questions, to characterise every criticism as rebellion, and to keep the abused in submission to their abusers. The results have been grievous: congregations manipulated, finances unexamined, sin covered, and the vulnerable told that God required their silence. Nothing in Scripture supports this, and several things in Scripture forbid it. Paul withstood Peter to the face and said so publicly (Galatians 2:11). The Bereans were commended for checking an apostle’s preaching against the Scriptures (Acts 17:11). Elders are to be examined before appointment and rebuked before all if they sin (1 Timothy 5:19– 20). The shepherds of God’s flock are explicitly forbidden to lord it over those in their charge (1 Peter 5:3). And the entire prophetic literature of the Old Testament consists of men sent by God to confront kings and priests. Nee himself submitted to a discipline he believed unjust, and did so for years without defending himself, which lends his teaching a moral weight it would otherwise lack. But the safeguard must be stated as plainly as the principle: authority is never a licence, and submission is never a substitute for truth. A leader who uses this doctrine to protect himself has, by that very act, stepped outside the authority he claims.

Where it is learned

Nee’s teaching on authority was given to full-time workers, but he was insistent that the training ground is not the ministry. It is the ordinary household. The New Testament bears this out. Every extended passage on authority in the epistles is domestic and occupational before it is ecclesiastical: wives and husbands, children and parents, servants and masters.

Servants, be obedient to them that are your masters according to the flesh, with fear and trembling, in singleness of your heart, as unto Christ; not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. EPHESIANS 6:5–6

Nee drew attention to the phrase not with eyeservice. The test of submission is what a man does when the authority is not watching. Work performed well only under observation is not obedience; it is management of appearances. He also noticed the extraordinary clause that follows in Colossians: and whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men (Colossians 3:23). The believer is never, finally, serving his employer. He is serving Christ through an arrangement Christ has permitted. This transforms ordinary work — and it also protects the worker, since a man whose real Master is in heaven cannot be owned by anyone on earth. Peter takes the same principle into genuinely difficult territory:

Servants, be subject to your masters with all fear; not only to the good and gentle, but also to the froward. 1 PETER 2:18

The froward — the crooked, the unreasonable. And Peter’s ground for this is not that the master deserves it, but that Christ endured injustice without retaliating and left us an example. Two things must be said to hold this rightly. The first is that Peter is describing an attitude within suffering, not a prohibition on seeking redress. Paul used his Roman citizenship and appealed to Caesar. A believer may lawfully leave a bad employer, report a crime, or seek protection. The second follows from the previous section of this chapter: nothing here authorises anyone to remain in danger. Where there is abuse, the biblical response is not silent endurance but rescue, and any teacher who uses these verses to keep a person in harm’s way has inverted their meaning entirely.

If you hold authority, ask whether you have ever used the language of submission to avoid being questioned. Repent of it specifically. 5. Where I must stand against what is wrong, give me courage without bitterness and firmness without pride. And where I hold any authority over others, guard me from ever using Your name to protect myself. Amen.

fields.body_html:
For as the body is one, and hath many members, and all the members of that one body, being many, are one body: so also is Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:12

Nee’s teaching on the church begins not with organisation, government or meetings, but with a fact he regarded as the great neglected revelation of the New Testament: the church is a Body, and a body is a living thing.

Not an illustration but a reality

He pressed hard on the last four words of the verse above. Paul builds his comparison — as the body is one and has many members — and then, where we expect him to conclude so also is the church, he writes so also is Christ. The Body is not a picture of the church. It is what the church is, and its life is Christ’s own.

And hath put all things under his feet, and gave him to be the head over all things to the church, which is his body, the fulness of him that filleth all in all. EPHESIANS 1:22–23

From this Nee drew a conclusion that governed all his thinking about church matters: you cannot organise a body. You may organise a machine, a company, an army. A body is not assembled; it grows, and it grows from a life already present within it. Every attempt to produce church life by structure alone is, on this view, an attempt to manufacture what only God can generate.

From whom the whole body fitly joined together and compacted by that which every joint supplieth, according to the effectual working in the measure of every part, maketh increase of the body unto the edifying of itself in love. EPHESIANS 4:16

The end of independence

The practical force of the Body doctrine, in Nee’s hands, was the demolition of the independent Christian.

And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:21

He observed that no member of a body functions for itself, and no member functions alone. A hand severed from the body retains its shape for a while and loses its usefulness immediately. Nee applied this to the private, self-sufficient Christianity that was already common in his day and is far commoner in ours — the believer who reads, prays, listens to preaching and answers to no one. Such a person, he argued, cannot grow properly, because growth is a Body function. He cannot see properly, because sight in spiritual things is given to the Body and mediated through it. And he cannot serve properly, because gifts are given not to individuals for their own use but to individuals for the Body’s sake.

But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:7

Learning to receive

There is an aspect of this that Nee emphasised more than most teachers, and it is worth dwelling on: the necessity of receiving from other members. Pride, he said, shows itself in ministry less by an unwillingness to give than by an unwillingness to receive. We are glad to help; we resent needing help. But if the Body is real, then God has deliberately distributed what I need into people I did not choose, may not like, and cannot control. To refuse them is to refuse Him. He connected this to the practice of fellowship in decision-making. A believer who has an impression about the Lord’s will does well, he taught, to bring it to the fellowship of mature brethren rather than acting alone — not because the brethren are infallible, but because the Body has a sense that no single member possesses.

One Body, and only one

Finally, Nee insisted that the Body’s unity is not an aspiration but a fact.

There is one body, and one Spirit, even as ye are called in one hope of your calling. EPHESIANS 4:4

We are not asked to create unity. We are asked to keep it: endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace (Ephesians 4:3). Division, on this view, is not the breaking of the Body — which cannot be broken — but the denial in practice of something that remains true in fact.

Whatever a reader concludes about Nee’s more particular views on church order, which we come to next, this much is beyond argument and profoundly practical: you cannot be a Christian by yourself. The New Testament does not envisage it, and God has arranged the supply of grace so that a believer who withdraws from the Body starves in the middle of plenty.

Gifts, ministries, and the measure of Christ

If the Body is real, what are the gifts for? Nee found the answer in a passage he treated as the charter of Christian ministry.

And he gave some, apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, pastors and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, for the edifying of the body of Christ. EPHESIANS 4:11–12

He laid stress on the purpose clause. The gifted men are given for the perfecting of the saints — the word suggests the setting of a bone, the mending of nets, the fitting of something for its function. Their business is not to do the work of the ministry on everyone else’s behalf. It is to equip the saints so that the saints do it. This underlay his hostility to a professional clergy, discussed further in the next chapter. Where one man performs and the rest observe, the arrangement is not merely inefficient; it prevents the Body from functioning and stunts every member in it. He also emphasised the goal towards which all this equipping runs:

Till we all come in the unity of the faith, and of the knowledge of the Son of God, unto a perfect man, unto the measure of the stature of the fulness of Christ. EPHESIANS 4:13

Till we all come. The destination is corporate. Nee took this to mean that no individual believer, however advanced, arrives on his own. The measure of the fullness of Christ is not attainable by a person; it is attainable by a Body. Which means that my growth is bound up with yours, and that the maturity of the whole is genuinely delayed by the immaturity of the parts. There is a sobering implication he did not shrink from. If the Body is real, my private sin is not private. It does not injure me alone.

And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it. 1 CORINTHIANS 12:26

And there is an encouraging implication too, which he pressed just as hard. My smallest faithful service is not small, because it is not mine alone either. The obscure member who prays, gives and endures unnoticed is supplying something to the whole that the whole cannot obtain elsewhere.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Name three believers you regularly receive from — not teach, not serve, but receive from. If you cannot name three, that is the finding.

2. Bring your next significant decision to two or three mature believers before you act, and genuinely listen. 3. Identify a member of your congregation you consider unnecessary. Ask God to show you what He has put in them for you. 4. Where you have contributed to division, take one concrete step of repair this month. 5. Ask what your gift is for. If the answer is chiefly your own fulfilment, reconsider.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are the Head, and I am a member — one among many, and not the most important.
Forgive my independence. I have prized being useful and resisted being needy. I have chosen which believers I would receive from, as though the supply were mine to arrange.
Join me truly to Your Body. Teach me to receive as freely as I give, to keep the unity You have already made, and to seek the profit of the whole rather than the enlargement of myself. Amen.

fields.title: The Church in the Place
fields.body_html:
Unto the church of God which is at Corinth …with all that in every place call upon the name of Jesus Christ our Lord. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:2

In 1938 Nee published the work known in English as The Normal Christian Church Life, sometimes titled Concerning Our Missions. It is his fullest treatment of church practice, and it is the part of his teaching about which believers most reasonably differ.

The observation

His argument begins with an observation about New Testament vocabulary that is difficult to dispute. Whenever the Scriptures speak of a church in a geographical sense, the identifier is always a place — never a doctrine, a founder, a practice or an emphasis. The church at Jerusalem, at Antioch, at Corinth, at Ephesus, at Philippi. The seven churches of Revelation are named for seven cities. There is no church of Peter, no church of the circumcision party, no church of those who prefer a particular view of the Lord’s Table. Further, Nee noted, the New Testament never speaks of two churches in one city, nor of one church spread over several cities. The unit is the locality, and within that locality every believer belongs. From this he concluded that division among Christians in the same town has no scriptural warrant whatsoever, and that the very existence of competing societies in one place — however orthodox each may be — is a departure from the apostolic pattern. He noted that when Paul confronted the Corinthians for saying I am of Paul; and I of Apollos; and I of Cephas, he did not merely reprove partisanship; he asked Is Christ divided? (1 Corinthians 1:12–13). His practical conclusion was that believers should gather simply as the church in their city, on no other ground than that they are Christians living there, receiving all whom Christ receives.

Wherefore receive ye one another, as Christ also received us to the glory of God. ROMANS 15:7

What follows from it

Several practical convictions flowed from this, and they shaped the assemblies that grew up under his ministry.

There should be no clergy-laity division, since the Body has many functioning members and no professional class. Elders are local and plural, raised up from among the believers rather than sent in. Apostles — or workers — travel, plant and build up, but do not govern the local churches or belong to them administratively. Meetings should allow for the contribution of the members rather than the performance of one man, on the pattern of when ye come together, every one of you hath a psalm, hath a doctrine (1 Corinthians 14:26). And the work should be supported by God’s provision rather than by solicitation. Whatever one makes of the whole system, several of these emphases have proved their worth in the hardest circumstances imaginable. When the state closed the church buildings in China, the assemblies that survived and multiplied were precisely those that had never depended on paid clergy, denominational structures or property.

Where careful believers differ

Honesty requires the other side, and it should not be softened. Many thoughtful Christians accept Nee’s exegetical observation and reject his conclusion. That the New Testament identifies churches by city may reflect the simple fact that in the first century there was only one Christian community in each city, rather than establishing a permanent law of church order. Descriptive history is not always prescriptive command, and Scripture nowhere states the principle in the form of a rule. There is also a practical difficulty that the principle carries within itself. If the ground of locality is what makes a gathering legitimate, then a group claiming that ground has implicitly denied it to everyone else in the town — and a doctrine devised to end division has become a new and particularly sharp instrument of it. This is not a hypothetical concern. In the movements that followed Nee, disputes over which gathering constituted the true church in a given city produced painful separations, and the history of that is not edifying. Nee himself, it should be said, was in practice more generous than the system might suggest; he received believers from many backgrounds and had warm fellowship with Christians who did not share his views on church ground.

How should an ordinary believer handle this chapter? Take the burden and hold the method loosely. The burden is real, and the New Testament shares it: that Christ has one Body, that our divisions grieve Him, that denominational loyalty must never outrank loyalty to Christ, and that we are obliged to receive every believer whom Christ has received. That much is not a matter of opinion.

That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us: that the world may believe that thou hast sent me. JOHN 17:21

Whether the remedy is a particular structure of gathering is another question altogether, and Christians of goodwill have answered it differently for a very long time.

What survived

There is a postscript to this chapter which no honest treatment can omit, because history has supplied a kind of commentary on it. When Watchman Nee was arrested in 1952, the assemblies he had served numbered some hundreds across China. Within a few years the buildings were closed, the leaders imprisoned or scattered, the literature destroyed, and public Christian worship as it had been known was effectively ended. During the Cultural Revolution the pressure intensified further. Foreign observers largely assumed that Chinese Protestantism had been extinguished. It had not. It would be an overstatement — and Nee would have disliked it — to credit this to any one man or movement. Many streams contributed, and much of the growth occurred among Christians who had never heard of him. But it is a matter of plain fact that the practices he had argued for from Scripture proved remarkably well suited to a church under a hostile state. A congregation with no building cannot have its building confiscated. A church with no salaried clergy cannot have its clergy defunded. A gathering in which every member can contribute does not collapse when one man is arrested. There is a lesson in this for believers in every place where the church may one day be pressed, which is to say in every place.

The persecution in Acts 8 destroyed the Jerusalem church as a single visible congregation and thereby spread the gospel across the region. What looked like the end of the work was its distribution. fields.title: The Ministry of Prayer
fields.body_html:
Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. MATTHEW 6:10

Nee returned to prayer throughout his ministry, and gathered his teaching on it in several places, notably Let Us Pray and the messages published as The Prayer Ministry of the Church. His treatment is distinctive because of the question he begins with. Most teaching on prayer asks how the believer may get what he needs from God. Nee asked something else: why does God need the believer to pray at all?

God has bound Himself to ask

His answer rests on the doctrine of authority in the earth. God gave dominion over this world to man (Genesis 1:26; Psalm 115:16). Man fell, and that dominion passed in practice to the usurper. In redemption, God works to recover the earth — and He does it, characteristically, not by sovereign fiat alone but through a redeemed humanity that wills what He wills. Hence, Nee argued, God has voluntarily limited Himself. He will do a great many things only when His people ask.

Ye have not, because ye ask not. JAMES 4:2
And he saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor. ISAIAH 59:16

He put it in a figure that has been much repeated: God’s will is like a train, and prayer is the track. The train has all the power; it goes nowhere without the rails. Prayer supplies no power at all — and without it the power does not arrive. This transforms what prayer is for. It is not chiefly a means of obtaining things. It is the agreement of the church with the will of God, by which His will is given a way into the earth.

Again I say unto you, That if two of you shall agree on earth as touching any thing that they shall ask, it shall be done for them of my Father which is in heaven. MATTHEW 18:19

Praying the will of God

It follows that the first labour of prayer is not speaking but discovering.

Nee taught believers to seek God’s mind before making requests, and he was unsparing about how much praying is merely the presentation of our own preferences with a religious ending attached. The Lord’s own pattern begins Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done — and only afterwards asks for bread.

And this is the confidence that we have in him, that, if we ask any thing according to his will, he heareth us. 1 JOHN 5:14

This is also, he noted, why the Spirit’s help is indispensable. We do not know what we should pray for, and the Spirit Himself makes intercession within us (Romans 8:26). Real prayer, on this understanding, originates in heaven, is carried by the Spirit into the heart of a believer, is prayed back to God, and is answered. The believer is the channel, not the source.

Authority in prayer

Nee distinguished several kinds of praying, and reserved particular emphasis for the prayer of authority — the prayer which, rather than pleading with God, speaks to the situation on the basis of Christ’s victory. He pointed to the Lord asleep in the boat. The disciples begged Him to save them; He got up and addressed the wind. He pointed to Moses at the Red Sea, told to stop crying out and to lift up his rod. And he pointed to the promise of the keys:

And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. MATTHEW 16:19

The church, seated with Christ, has been given the authority to declare on earth what heaven has already determined. But Nee guarded this immediately, and the guard is essential: such prayer is only valid within the will of God, and only from a position of submission. A believer who has not learned obedience has no authority to exercise, and attempting it is presumption.

Persistence, and the discipline of it

Finally, he taught persistence without anxiety. The widow before the unjust judge, the friend at midnight, Elijah sending his servant seven times to look at an empty sky — these are given us not because God is reluctant but because prayer is warfare and warfare takes time.

Pray without ceasing. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:17

And practically, Nee urged the keeping of records — specific requests, dates, answers. Vague praying, he observed, produces vague faith, and a believer who never asks for anything definite will never know whether God has answered.

Praise before the answer

There is one further form of praying which Nee treated as belonging to the highest order, and it is the one most of us reach for last.

And when he had consulted with the people, he appointed singers unto the Lord, and that should praise the beauty of holiness, as they went out before the army, and to say, Praise the Lord; for his mercy endureth for ever. 2 CHRONICLES 20:21

Jehoshaphat’s position was hopeless by any military reckoning, and his own prayer had admitted it — neither know we what to do: but our eyes are upon thee (2 Chronicles 20:12). What he did next was to put the choir in front of the soldiers. The praise went out before the battle, not after the victory. Nee’s point was not that praise is a technique for obtaining results. He was firm about that; the moment praise is offered in order to make something happen it has become a transaction and ceased to be worship. The point is what praise declares. To thank God before the answer arrives is to state, in the most practical way available, that the matter is already settled with Him. He pointed also to a Philippian prison at midnight, where two men with bleeding backs and their feet in the stocks sang hymns loudly enough that the other prisoners listened (Acts 16:25). The earthquake came afterwards. The singing was not caused by the deliverance; it preceded it, and it happened in circumstances that offered no encouragement whatever.

By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name. HEBREWS 13:15

The word sacrifice is exact. Praise offered when everything is well costs nothing. Praise offered in the dark costs something, which is precisely what makes it an offering. Nee’s counsel, given to people about to endure a good deal, was to make thanksgiving a discipline rather than a mood: to begin prayer with it, to practise it in trouble specifically, and to refuse to wait for circumstances to justify it.

In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:18

In every thing, he was careful to note — not for every thing. We are not asked to call evil good. We are asked to find God present in the middle of it, and to say so.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Begin your praying this week by asking what God wants, and spend as long listening as asking. 2. Keep a written list of specific requests with dates. Review it monthly and record the answers. 3. Find one other believer and agree together, in Matthew 18 fashion, on one definite matter. 4. Where you have been begging God to do what He has already accomplished in Christ, change your posture: thank Him, and stand. 5. Examine your prayers for a week. What proportion concerned your comfort, and what proportion concerned His kingdom?

A PRAYER
Father, You have chosen to work through the prayers of Your people, and I have often left the rails unlaid.
Forgive me for prayers that were only my own wishes with Your name attached. Teach me to seek Your mind before I open my mouth.
Holy Spirit, pray in me what I do not know how to pray. Give me the persistence that does not let go, and the submission without which authority is only presumption. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done. Amen.

fields.title: The Overcomers and the Reward
fields.body_html:
To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne. REVELATION 3:21

The last strand of Nee’s teaching to consider is the one that gave his movement its urgency and its name for suffering. It is the doctrine of the overcomers, set out most fully in the addresses published as God’s Plan and the Overcomers, and running through much of what he wrote about the kingdom and the church.

God’s eternal purpose

Nee began not with the fall but with the purpose that preceded it. God’s intention, declared in Genesis 1:26, was a race bearing His image and exercising His dominion. Sin interrupted it; redemption serves it. Salvation, in his framing, is not the end of God’s plan but the means by which the original purpose is recovered.

According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord. EPHESIANS 3:11

The consummation is a corporate one: a Body prepared, a Bride made ready, a city descending.

The overcomers

But Nee observed something about the way God has always worked. When the whole fails, God takes a remnant, and through the remnant recovers the whole. Noah in the flood. The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal. Gideon’s three hundred. The returning exiles under Zerubbabel. He applied this to the church. The Lord’s word to the seven churches of Asia is addressed to whole congregations, but the promise is invariably narrowed: to him that overcometh. Not to the church as a whole — to those within it who overcome.

He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. REVELATION 21:7

The overcomers, in Nee’s teaching, are not a superior class of Christian with a different salvation. They are simply the believers who are actually living the normal Christian life — those in whom the cross has done its work — and God uses them to secure His purpose for the whole Body.

Salvation and reward

Here Nee made his most controversial eschatological distinction, and it must be set out accurately and then examined. He held — following Robert Govett, G. H. Pember and D. M. Panton, whose works he had absorbed early — that Scripture distinguishes between salvation, which is by grace through faith and cannot be lost, and reward, which is according to works and can be forfeited. Every believer will be saved. Not every believer will reign.

If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:14–15
For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:10

From this he taught that some believers will enter the coming kingdom’s reign and others will not, that the millennial reign is a reward rather than a universal Christian entitlement, and that a believer may suffer real loss — though never the loss of salvation itself.

Weighing it

The distinction between salvation and reward is plainly biblical. The passages above teach it, and so do the parables of the talents and the pounds. Believers who ignore it tend towards a complacency the New Testament never permits. But the further elaboration — a partial rapture, exclusion of some believers from the millennial kingdom, a period of remedial discipline for the unfaithful — rests on a chain of inferences rather than on plain statements, and the majority of evangelical interpreters have not been persuaded. These are matters on which sincere believers have disagreed for a long time, and the wise reader will hold them lightly. What should not be held lightly is the moral point beneath them, which is unmistakably apostolic: how a Christian lives now will matter then.

But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:27

There is something fitting in ending here, because this doctrine was not theoretical for the man who taught it.

Watchman Nee spoke about the overcomers to workers who would shortly be scattered, imprisoned and in some cases killed. He himself spent the last twenty years of his life in confinement, refusing his freedom on the terms offered. He was denounced by former colleagues, buried his wife without being permitted to attend, and died on a labour farm in Anhwei with a piece of paper under his pillow affirming that Christ is the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again, and that he still believed it. He had preached that the crown goes to those who overcome. He was required to prove whether he meant it.

Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. REVELATION 2:10

The Bride made ready

Nee’s overcomer teaching has an end in view, and it is not individual. He set it out most fully in The Glorious Church, tracing a single thread from the first pages of Scripture to the last. He began at Eden, with a detail he considered deliberate. Eve was not formed separately from the dust as Adam had been; she was taken out of the man, from his opened side, while a deep sleep was upon him.

And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs …and the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman. GENESIS 2:21–22

In this Nee saw a foreshadowing of the last Adam, from whose opened side on the cross came the church — a bride of the same nature as the Bridegroom, drawn out of His death.

Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it …that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing. EPHESIANS 5:25–27

The consummation, then, is a wedding.

Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. REVELATION 19:7

Two words in that verse carried Nee’s whole burden. Made herself ready — there is something the Bride does, and it is not automatic. And his wife, singular — the readiness is corporate. There is no such thing as an individual bride. This is where the overcomer teaching finds its proper proportion, and it guards against the misuse the doctrine invites. The overcomers are not a spiritual elite being rewarded for outperforming their brethren. They are those in whom God has been able to do His work, and the purpose of that work is not their private distinction but the readiness of the whole. They are the firstfruits, not the harvest; the vanguard, not the destination. Understood that way, the doctrine produces exactly the opposite of spiritual competition. A man who grasps it does not ask how he may be counted among the overcomers. He asks what it will cost him to be of use to the Body, and he stops keeping score — which is, in Nee’s terms, a fair sign that the cross has begun its work.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Live this week with the judgment seat of Christ genuinely in view. Let it affect one specific decision. 2. Distinguish clearly in your own mind between what is settled — your salvation — and what is not yet settled: your faithfulness. 3. Identify one area where you are building with wood, hay and stubble — activity that will not survive the fire. Stop, or rebuild it. 4. Hold the disputed details lightly and the moral urgency tightly. Do not divide from anyone over the finer points of the kingdom. 5. Ask what you would refuse to surrender if it cost you your liberty. Then ask whether you are living now as though that were true.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You are coming, and I will stand before You, and the fire will test what I have built.
I thank You that my salvation is not in question — it rests wholly on Your finished work. But my faithfulness is very much in question, and I ask You to deal with me now rather than to leave it until then.
Make me an overcomer, not for the honour of it, but because You are worthy of a people who did not love their lives unto the death. Whatever it costs, keep me faithful to the end. Amen.
fields.body_text: To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne. REVELATION 3:21 The last strand of Nee’s teaching to consider is the one that gave his movement its urgency and its name for suffering. It is the doctrine of the overcomers, set out most fully in the addresses published as God’s Plan and the Overcomers, and running through much of what he wrote about the kingdom and the church. God’s eternal purpose Nee began not with the fall but with the purpose that preceded it. God’s intention, declared in Genesis 1:26, was a race bearing His image and exercising His dominion. Sin interrupted it; redemption serves it. Salvation, in his framing, is not the end of God’s plan but the means by which the original purpose is recovered. According to the eternal purpose which he purposed in Christ Jesus our Lord. EPHESIANS 3:11 The consummation is a corporate one: a Body prepared, a Bride made ready, a city descending. The overcomers But Nee observed something about the way God has always worked. When the whole fails, God takes a remnant, and through the remnant recovers the whole. Noah in the flood. The seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal. Gideon’s three hundred. The returning exiles under Zerubbabel. He applied this to the church. The Lord’s word to the seven churches of Asia is addressed to whole congregations, but the promise is invariably narrowed: to him that overcometh. Not to the church as a whole — to those within it who overcome. He that overcometh shall inherit all things; and I will be his God, and he shall be my son. REVELATION 21:7 The overcomers, in Nee’s teaching, are not a superior class of Christian with a different salvation. They are simply the believers who are actually living the normal Christian life — those in whom the cross has done its work — and God uses them to secure His purpose for the whole Body. Salvation and reward Here Nee made his most controversial eschatological distinction, and it must be set out accurately and then examined. He held — following Robert Govett, G. H. Pember and D. M. Panton, whose works he had absorbed early — that Scripture distinguishes between salvation, which is by grace through faith and cannot be lost, and reward, which is according to works and can be forfeited. Every believer will be saved. Not every believer will reign. If any man’s work abide which he hath built thereupon, he shall receive a reward. If any man’s work shall be burned, he shall suffer loss: but he himself shall be saved; yet so as by fire. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:14–15 For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ; that every one may receive the things done in his body, according to that he hath done, whether it be good or bad. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:10 From this he taught that some believers will enter the coming kingdom’s reign and others will not, that the millennial reign is a reward rather than a universal Christian entitlement, and that a believer may suffer real loss — though never the loss of salvation itself. Believers who ignore it tend towards a complacency the New Testament never permits. But the further elaboration — a partial rapture, exclusion of some believers from the millennial kingdom, a period of remedial discipline for the unfaithful — rests on a chain of inferences rather than on plain statements, and the majority of evangelical interpreters have not been persuaded. These are matters on which sincere believers have disagreed for a long time, and the wise reader will hold them lightly. What should not be held lightly is the moral point beneath them, which is unmistakably apostolic: how a Christian lives now will matter then. But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:27 There is something fitting in ending here, because this doctrine was not theoretical for the man who taught it. Watchman Nee spoke about the overcomers to workers who would shortly be scattered, imprisoned and in some cases killed. He himself spent the last twenty years of his life in confinement, refusing his freedom on the terms offered. He was denounced by former colleagues, buried his wife without being permitted to attend, and died on a labour farm in Anhwei with a piece of paper under his pillow affirming that Christ is the Son of God who died for sinners and rose again, and that he still believed it. He had preached that the crown goes to those who overcome. He was required to prove whether he meant it. Be thou faithful unto death, and I will give thee a crown of life. He set it out most fully in The Glorious Church, tracing a single thread from the first pages of Scripture to the last. He began at Eden, with a detail he considered deliberate. Eve was not formed separately from the dust as Adam had been; she was taken out of the man, from his opened side, while a deep sleep was upon him. And the Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs …and the rib, which the Lord God had taken from man, made he a woman. GENESIS 2:21–22 In this Nee saw a foreshadowing of the last Adam, from whose opened side on the cross came the church — a bride of the same nature as the Bridegroom, drawn out of His death. Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it …that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing. EPHESIANS 5:25–27 The consummation, then, is a wedding. Let us be glad and rejoice, and give honour to him: for the marriage of the Lamb is come, and his wife hath made herself ready. REVELATION 19:7 Two words in that verse carried Nee’s whole burden. Made herself ready — there is something the Bride does, and it is not automatic. And his wife, singular — the readiness is corporate. There is no such thing as an individual bride. This is where the overcomer teaching finds its proper proportion, and it guards against the misuse the doctrine invites. The overcomers are not a spiritual elite being rewarded for outperforming their brethren. They are those in whom God has been able to do His work, and the purpose of that work is not their private distinction but the readiness of the whole. They are the firstfruits, not the harvest; the vanguard, not the destination. Understood that way, the doctrine produces exactly the opposite of spiritual competition. A man who grasps it does not ask how he may be counted among the overcomers. He asks what it will cost him to be of use to the Body, and he stops keeping score — which is, in Nee’s terms, a fair sign that the cross has begun its work. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Live this week with the judgment seat of Christ genuinely in view. Let it affect one specific decision. 2. Distinguish clearly in your own mind between what is settled — your salvation — and what is not yet settled: your faithfulness. 3. Identify one area where you are building with wood, hay and stubble — activity that will not survive the fire. Stop, or rebuild it. 4. Hold the disputed details lightly and the moral urgency tightly. Do not divide from anyone over the finer points of the kingdom. 5. Ask what you would refuse to surrender if it cost you your liberty. Then ask whether you are living now as though that were true.
