fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
He must increase, but I must decrease. JOHN 3:30

We have covered a great deal of ground in eighteen short chapters, and it would be easy to close this book with the impression that Watchman Nee taught many things. In truth he taught one thing, from many angles, for thirty years. The one thing is this: Christ has done everything, and the believer’s whole business is to get out of the way. Everything else is commentary. The distinction between the blood and the cross is that truth applied to guilt and to nature. Know, reckon, present is that truth applied to the mechanics of daily deliverance. Sit, walk, stand is that truth applied to position, conduct and conflict. The breaking of the outer man is that truth applied to the servant. The Body is that truth applied to the church. And the overcomers are simply those in whom it has been allowed to work.

What to do with it

If you have read this far, you are now in a position of some danger. Nee himself would have said so. The peculiar hazard of teaching about the deeper life is that it can be received as a subject. A man may become an enthusiast for the doctrine of the cross while remaining entirely uncrucified. He may collect the vocabulary — reckoning, brokenness, soul-life, the Body — and deploy it fluently, and be exactly the same man he was before, only harder to help. Nothing in these pages is of the slightest use as information.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So here is the plainest counsel this book can give. Go back to the one chapter that made you uncomfortable. Not the one you found most interesting — the one you would rather not read again. That is where God is working. Take the application points at the end of it, and do them, one at a time, slowly, over the coming months. Then take the next. And expect it to be unspectacular. The great danger of a book like this is that it creates an appetite for crisis — for a single overwhelming experience after which everything is different. Such moments do occur; Nee’s ministry contains several. But the ordinary shape of this work is far less dramatic. It is a long succession of small surrenders, most of them unwitnessed, in which a man gradually stops defending himself.

Two things to carry

Carry away, first, a settled confidence. If you take nothing else from these chapters, take this: your acceptance with God does not fluctuate. It was established at Calvary, it rests on the blood of Christ, and your performance this week did not improve it and cannot damage it. Every genuine advance in the Christian life begins from that security, never from anxiety about it. Carry away, second, a holy discontent with the ordinary. Not with your circumstances — Nee had rather more to be discontented about than most of us and did not complain — but with the gap between what Scripture says is normal and what we have settled for. That discontent, honestly held before God, is one of the surest signs that the Spirit is at work.

Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 3:12

A last word about the man

We have been honest in these pages about Watchman Nee’s limitations. He speculated where Scripture is silent. He systematised what might have been left as testimony. Parts of his teaching have been used, by others and perhaps sometimes by himself, in ways that did harm. His life contains a period of withdrawal he never fully explained and accusations that will not be settled in this world. None of that has been raised in order to diminish him. It has been raised because he taught, more insistently than almost anyone, that no servant of God is to be looked at. The man who wrote about the alabaster box would have been appalled to become one. And so the right response to his ministry is not admiration. It is obedience — not to him, but to the Lord he pointed at, whose life he spent thirty years trying to describe and twenty years quietly proving.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith. HEBREWS 12:2

The watchman’s work is to wake the household and then to be forgotten. He would be content with that.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I have read about Your cross, and I have understood some of it, and I am afraid of leaving it there.
Do not let me become a student of the deeper life instead of a partaker of it. Do not let me acquire words for things I have never experienced.
Take the truth I have seen and press it into me until it costs me something. Begin with the chapter I would rather forget. Begin today.
You must increase. I must decrease. Amen.

fields.title: A Reader’s Guide to Watchman Nee
fields.body_html:
Study to shew thyself approved unto God, a workman that needeth not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. 2 TIMOTHY 2:15

Nee wrote comparatively little with his own pen. Most of what bears his name consists of spoken addresses taken down by hearers and afterwards edited, translated and published — sometimes long after his death, and in more than one competing English version. Readers should therefore hold particular sentences loosely, especially where a point turns on precise wording. What follows is a guide for further reading, arranged for usefulness rather than chronology.

Begin here

The Normal Christian Life. His best-known book and the natural starting place, drawn from addresses given in Europe in 1938 and 1939 and compiled by Angus Kinnear. An exposition of Romans, and the source of the know–reckon–present–obey sequence treated in chapters four to six of this book. Sit, Walk, Stand. Very short, and arguably his most perfectly constructed work. An exposition of Ephesians in three movements. If you have an hour, spend it here. The Release of the Spirit (also published as The Breaking of the Outer Man and the Release of the Spirit). Brief, searching, and the book most likely to do you good if you are in Christian work.

For deeper study

The Spiritual Man, three volumes, 1928. His earliest major work, written during severe illness, setting out the spirit–soul–body framework discussed in chapter eleven. Thorough and demanding. Nee himself came to think it over-systematised; read it with that caution. Spiritual Authority. From the Kuling trainings of 1948–49. Powerful, and to be read alongside 1 Peter 5 and the cautions given in chapter fourteen of this book. The Character of God’s Workman and The Ministry of God’s Word. Also from the Kuling period. Addressed to those who preach; unusually practical about the moral qualifications of a servant. What Shall This Man Do? On the three ministries typified by Peter, Paul and John — the fisherman, the builder, the mender. Valuable for understanding differing callings.

Church and corporate life

The Normal Christian Church Life (originally Concerning Our Missions, 1938). His treatment of church order, apostles, elders and the ground of locality. The material behind chapter sixteen. Read critically. Assembling Together. More practical and less controversial: on baptism, the Lord’s Table, laying on of hands and the conduct of meetings. The Glorious Church. On the church as the bride, tracing the theme from Eve through to the New Jerusalem. Some of his most imaginative writing, with the strengths and risks that implies.

Devotional

A Table in the Wilderness. A daily devotional compiled from his ministry. The gentlest introduction to him, and a good gift. Changed into His Likeness. On Abraham, Isaac and Jacob as pictures of God’s dealings with a man. Warm and pastoral. Love Not the World. A short, sharp treatment of the world system. The Song of Songs. His devotional exposition, in the tradition of the mystics he read.

Approach with discernment

The Latent Power of the Soul (1933). Discussed at length in chapter thirteen. Not recommended for a new believer, and not to be read without the qualifications set out there. God’s Plan and the Overcomers, and other material on the kingdom and rewards. The salvation–reward distinction is scriptural; the further eschatological structure is disputed. Read alongside standard evangelical treatments of the same passages.

About Watchman Nee

Against the Tide by Angus Kinnear is the standard sympathetic biography, written by the man who edited The Normal Christian Life. Watchman Nee: A Seer of the Divine Revelation presents the view of the movement that continued through Witness Lee. For a more critical scholarly assessment, consult the entry in the Biographical Dictionary of Chinese Christianity and standard histories of twentieth-century Chinese Protestantism. Reading more than one of these is strongly advised; no single account is disinterested.

A closing note on how to read him

Three counsels, offered in the spirit of 1 Thessalonians 5:21.

Read him with the Bible open, and check every claim. He would have insisted on it. Read him for the burden rather than the system. Where he presses a framework beyond what Scripture states, take the pastoral concern and leave the scaffolding. And read him slowly. These are not books to be finished. A page a day, prayed over, will do more than a volume a week admired.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21
